entries.question: What is the difference between AGI, the singularity, and superintelligence?
entries.body:
_Three different ideas that boardrooms constantly conflate, with the founder who coined "AGI" drawing the lines._

> A truly general intelligence should be able to figure out how to achieve any goal in any environment. To be an AGI you should be able to pivot beyond whatever you were programmed for: given an unfamiliar environment and an unfamiliar goal, figure out on the fly, with creative imagination and trial and error, how to achieve it. The singularity is a point at which the rate of progress in AI, biotech, nanotech and space becomes so fast it would feel infinite to a legacy human being like us.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Why is doing 95% of human jobs not the same as AGI?
entries.body:
_Automating most work would be hugely valuable, but value is not the same as general intelligence._

> When Sam Altman says his definition of AGI is an AI that can do 95% of human jobs, that's really not it. If you could make a system to do 95% of human jobs but it does it just by copying a huge amount of training data that contains a million examples of each job, that may be incredibly valuable and have immense humanitarian value, but it's not making big leaps of generalization beyond its training data, so it's not an AGI.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Are large language models the path to AGI, or an off-ramp?
entries.body:
_LLMs are powerful and useful, but scaling them may be a detour rather than the road to general intelligence._

> I don't think LLMs are AGI, nor that fully scaling up LLMs is going to get you to AGI. I sort of agree with Yann LeCun that on the path to AGI, LLMs are an off-ramp. I still think we can get there by 2029 or even sooner, because the pace of progress is just insane and there are a lot of other techniques now being tried at smaller scale.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: What are the core limitations of transformers and backpropagation for building AGI?
entries.body:
_The train-then-freeze design of today's models is the wrong shape for a mind that keeps learning._

> Because of the underlying backpropagation algorithm, learning and inference are separate phases. You train a model, you freeze it, and then you use it. If you try to fill the network up with knowledge and keep going, at some point you get catastrophic forgetting: adding a little new knowledge causes it to forget a lot of old knowledge. These systems know a lot, but they don't reorganize themselves in real time the way parts of the human brain do.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: What is predictive coding and why does it matter for AGI?
entries.body:
_Changing the learning rule, not just the architecture, may be what unlocks continual learning._

> There's something called predictive coding which more closely resembles how the brain works. On smaller neural nets, predictive coding networks are better at continual learning: they don't have as much catastrophic forgetting, each neuron can learn asynchronously and independently, and you can do inference and learning in the same phase. The need for hyperscaler server farms is less, because the learning is asynchronous.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: What is the neuro-symbolic approach to AGI behind OpenCog Hyperon?
entries.body:
_Goertzel's own bet replaces the neural net as the core data structure with a self-modifying knowledge graph that fuses neural, logical, and evolutionary learning._

> The basic data structure isn't a neural net, it's a huge dynamic self-modifying knowledge graph living in RAM across multiple machines. You can put neural nets in there, you can put logical propositions in there and do theorem proving, and you can put program code in there and evolve it with genetic programming that simulates evolution by natural selection. Then you wrap a goal-driven cognitive architecture around it.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Why would superintelligence follow quickly after human-level AGI?
entries.body:
_Once a machine can rewrite its own code, the leap from human-level to superhuman may be far shorter than the leap to human-level._

> If you have a human-level AGI in 2029, it is going to be able to optimize its own code and analyze its own foundations and exceed the human level in much less than the sixteen-year gap Kurzweil drew between AGI and superintelligence. This is recursive self-improvement: the AI makes a smarter AI, makes a smarter AI. We're actually designing Hyperon precisely for recursive self-improvement, which the human brain never evolved to do.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Where do neuro-symbolic AI systems beat large language models today?
entries.body:
_The clearest near-term edge for non-LLM AI is messy data that is part numbers, part narrative._

> When you have data that is a mix of quantitative and qualitative in a confusing, tangled-up way, LLMs are not great at sifting through the structured part at scale. Medical data is like this: a lot of qualitative information plus hard clinical numbers. Many areas of finance are like this. I've worked on catastrophic risk estimation, like how to price the risk of a revolution in a developing country. That's where symbolic reasoning plus creative leaps, with an LLM there to crunch the text, has a big advantage.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: How should businesses prepare for AGI, and what comes after chatbots and agents?
entries.body:
_The practical move is to avoid overcommitting and to build toward agents with persistent memory rather than one-shot chatbots._

> The right answer is not to overcommit to any particular technology at a particular moment, because if the singularity idea is at all real, we're all going to have to pivot and re-pivot. What's coming is agents with persistent memory that reason on that memory and build their own world model as they go. An agent that remembers everything it ever did feels less like a query loop and more like a personal assistant you actually have a relationship with.

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: What is the economic risk during the transition to AGI?
entries.body:
_The dangerous window may not be an evil superintelligence, but the gap between AGI that can automate jobs and superintelligence that can deliver abundance._

> What worries me is the period after you have the first human-level AGI but before you have a superintelligence that can bring massive abundance. You've got an AGI that can in principle automate almost any job and is crunching through one industry after another, but you don't yet have the superintelligence that can airdrop a molecular nano-assembler in everyone's backyard. What happens to the world economy in that interval? Who gives universal basic income in the Central African Republic?

Source: [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052826/)

entries.question: Why is detecting cancer early the biggest lever in treatment?
entries.body:
_The survival math changes completely with the stage at which cancer is found._

> The biggest lever is to treat cancer early. Lung cancer is the number one killer of all cancers, it kills twice as many people as the second biggest. If you detect it at stage one, you have over a 60% survival rate after five years. If you detect it at stage four, you have an 8% chance of living five years from now, 92% will die. You can only treat it early if you diagnose it early.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: What is the core problem with today's cancer drugs?
entries.body:
_Even the best cancer drugs are imprecise, and the imprecision forces a dose that limits how well they work._

> The number one problem with cancer drugs is systemic toxicity. When you dose someone, the drug doesn't only work on the tumor, it also works on healthy cells. That's why your hair falls out in chemotherapy. The top 10 cancer drugs produce 87 billion dollars a year, and on average they give you 12 months more to live and 15 percentage points more survival, which gets you to 49% in total, meaning every second person still dies.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: How can a cancer cell be made to produce its own drug?
entries.body:
_The aim is a therapy produced by the tumor, against the tumor, in the tumor, so potent drugs stay local._

> We created the first genetic switches made out of DNA that only turn on in cancer cells. You inject them and they go everywhere, but they only flip on inside a cancer cell, like a light switch. We only get into about 1% of the cancer cells, so the cell produces a message, a smoke signal, that brings the immune system to attack the rest, like a domino chain reaction. The hard part is keeping all of it inside the tumor so you avoid off-target effects.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: What is the 'billion dollar barrier' in delivering gene therapies?
entries.body:
_Getting genetic cargo to a tumor, and not to the liver, has blocked the field for 15 years._

> Somehow you have to get this DNA to the tumor, and that's where lipid nanoparticles come in. You've probably already had them in a COVID vaccine. The problem is that within 10 minutes they're in your liver and out of your body, because the liver flushes out everything that doesn't belong. So to treat any cancer other than liver cancer you need a completely different lipid nanoparticle. For 15 years that has been called the billion dollar barrier.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Why did the first AI approach to designing cancer switches fail, and how was it fixed?
entries.body:
_What works on lab cell lines can collapse on real patient samples, and the fix was to change the question._

> The original concept used a switch that nature provides, an endogenous promoter. It looked really good in cell lines that never change in the lab, but the moment we tried it on individual real cancer patient samples from the operating room, the whole thing failed completely. So instead of interrogating every single mutation, we asked the opposite question and looked at the downstream commonalities, the hallmarks of cancer, and identified master transcription factor binding sites that are dysregulated.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: How can a large language model design DNA for new cancer drugs?
entries.body:
_DNA is a four-letter text, which makes sequence design a next-token problem, but only with the right data and a tight feedback loop._

> What is DNA? It's text. The alphabet of DNA has four letters and they keep permutating, so it's a perfect problem for an LLM, if it's trained on the right data. The general models are only okay-ish for DNA. There's one trained specifically on DNA, Evo 2 by the Arc Institute, the best out there, but still 99% of what comes out is useless. So we built a proprietary Oracle to predict what is not useless, feed it to the wet lab, and the outliers go back into the model. Every spin of the wheel, it gets smarter.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Why are fine-tuned models on proprietary data the real moat, not another foundation model?
entries.body:
_The same transformer everyone has becomes a defensible asset only when trained on data nobody else holds._

> Cyriac uses the same transformer that is the basis for AI generally, but he trains it on data from his own wet lab that nobody else has, to get a fine-tuned model that can answer questions nobody else can. The future right now is really fine-tuned models trained on specific data nobody else has. There is a race on data and a race on fine-tuned models, and the same underlying idea is happening in every industry across the globe.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

sources.title: Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)

entries.question: Why does physical AI need real physical-world data?
entries.body:
_Models that act on the physical world are only as good as the real-world data they are trained on._

> Physical AI is only interesting when you train it on physical-world data. All models need real data, and the physical world models need real-world data. So in biology, you need a wet lab with pipettes and a vivarium with mice, and you have to generate high-quality data, because otherwise it's garbage in, garbage out.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

entries.question: How should executives decide where to apply AI?
entries.body:
_Start with the problem, not the tool, and the right use of AI emerges on its own._

> You don't start with the tool, you start with the problem, and then it naturally emerges which tools are best to use. If you want a house, you start with wanting the house, then find the materials and skilled people. You don't start with a screwdriver and ask what you could build with it. AI is like suddenly having a bazooka in your toolbox: it's incredibly powerful, but you still need to aim it and know exactly what to do with it.

Source: [Tomorrow's Medicine, with Cyriac Roeding (eCornell Keynote)](https://ecornell.cornell.edu/keynotes/view/K052126/)

entries.question: What did Jim Allison's checkpoint inhibitors miss, and how does early aim to complete the picture?
entries.body:
_Releasing the immune system's brake was a Nobel-winning breakthrough, but a brake release alone does not move the car._

> Checkpoint inhibitors are the biggest cancer innovation in the last 20 years, and Jim Allison won the Nobel Prize in 2018 for the insight that you first have to take the foot off the brake of the immune system. But even the best of them have on average a 35% response rate. The problem is, if you take your foot off the brake but never push the gas, the car doesn't move. You also have to stimulate the immune system, and we do that locally at the tumor. That is the second missing piece of the puzzle.

entries.question: What is an AI agent, really?
entries.body:
_Not a sci-fi character, a workflow that chains steps._

An agent is not a sci-fi character and it is not one giant model. It is a piece of code that takes a defined task, breaks it into steps, and lets you act on software through language. The core idea is chaining: instead of asking a model to "improve revenue," you break the goal into step one, step two, step three, exactly the way a manager hands work to a junior employee. Tools like LangChain popularized this. So an agent is less a breakthrough model than a workflow that combines models, tools, and sometimes plain deterministic code, each doing one step.

— [The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-12-12-ai-agents-the-future-of-work/) · _Podcast_

entries.question: How are AI agents different from RPA (robotic process automation)?
entries.body:
_Agents add reasoning where RPA's rule engine stops._

RPA is a rule engine. It automates structured, low-skilled tasks where every decision is essentially zero or one, which is why UiPath and Automation Anywhere built real businesses but hit a ceiling: a script either breaks or runs, and it cannot handle uncertainty or unstructured data. Agents add a language model on top, so they can read an email's style, cope with ambiguity, and self-correct. Cherry's portfolio company Octomind does this for front-end testing with a self-healing loop that notices when a test goes wrong and tries another path, something a rule engine cannot do. The catch: you still have to give an agent clear boundaries, or it goes rogue.

— [The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-12-12-ai-agents-the-future-of-work/) · _Podcast_

sources.title: The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”

entries.question: What patterns make a workflow 'agentic' rather than just a wrapper around an LLM?
entries.body:
_Reflection, self-correction, knowledge expansion, coordination._

A few recurring patterns. Reflection: the system plans, asks "is this approach good, does this make sense, can you double-check," and only then executes, the way a reasoning model breaks a request into several approaches, picks one, and verifies the answer. Self-correction: it looks at the result, notices it went wrong, and tries a different route. Knowledge expansion: when the answer is not in its memory, it searches the web for current information. Coordination: it splits a job into sub-tasks and routes each to the right tool, for example handing a math question to a calculator instead of guessing. Wrapping a chat box around an LLM is none of these.

— [The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-12-12-ai-agents-the-future-of-work/) · _Podcast_

sources.title: The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”

entries.question: If agents are the future, why won't one giant model just do everything?
entries.body:
_The moat is the workflow, not a bigger model._

Because the durable approach is the opposite: smaller, faster, specialized models orchestrated together, not one ever-bigger general model. Even OpenAI orchestrates the long tail of consumer search with smaller models, because a big model would be far too slow. For founders this is the key warning: if your agent's next step is something generic, like deciding whether a calculator is needed, that is the long tail, and the big models will absorb it, just as Google eventually swallowed the specialized search engines. The defensible business is one where the founder knows the specific stepwise workflow of a domain and chains the right models and rules to serve it.

— [The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-12-12-ai-agents-the-future-of-work/) · _Podcast_

entries.question: Why can't I just tell an agent to plan my honeymoon or buy things for me?
entries.body:
_Match the agent to the stakes._

Technically you can wire it up, but it will not be trusted yet, and for good reason. The blocker is not hallucination, which is largely a solved technical problem, it is stakes and trust: people do not want an agent that might book the wrong flight or charge the wrong thing to their card. The honest pattern is to match the agent to the stakes. Lutz started by imagining a health "nurse in your pocket," found the stakes too high to be reliable, and moved to lower-stakes commerce like helping someone find the right ring or coffee machine, where an agentic workflow that cleans the data and searches step by step adds value without the risk. High precision with an agent is possible; you scope it to where a mistake is survivable.

— [The Edge: “AI Agents: The Future of Work?”](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-12-12-ai-agents-the-future-of-work/) · _Podcast_

entries.question: Why is measuring social media so difficult despite all the tools available today?
entries.body:
_Tools are everywhere, but strategy comes first, not scores._

The problem is that measurement used to require specialists with big databases and tooling. Now with social media, you suddenly have all these tools that give you cloud scores and metrics instantly. People see a score and decide something based on it without planning what they actually want to achieve. If you haven't formulated your business goal first, any measurement won't work. People start with the measurement and then think about what to do with it, while the correct way is the opposite: start with a question, then come up with a measure.

entries.question: What is the difference between virality and contagiousness?
entries.body:
_Stories gain weight as they travel, not uniform infection rates._

Virality is something which is equally infectious at each stage. If I have a story which one out of 10 people like, that story doesn't change. One out of 10 people like it in the future as well. Contagiousness is different. As long as it travels, it gains weight. The more people believe in it, the more trustworthy the story becomes. Even a wrong information becomes more believed the longer it travels. At some point everyone believes it's truth no matter what because so many people believed in it. Forget about virality. The right word is contagiousness.

entries.question: How does AI change the way we interact with computers compared to previous interfaces?
entries.body:
_From punch cards to conversation: AI as natural interface_

AI enables me to communicate with machines using natural language instead of learning complex commands or navigating graphical interfaces. Previously, we evolved from punch cards to MS-DOS commands to graphical interfaces with mice and clicking. Each step made things more intuitive, but I still had to search and learn the system's rules. Now with large language models, I can simply describe what I want in my own words. The AI understands my intent and produces output, even if I have no idea how it works technically. This is revolutionary because humans naturally communicate through language.

— [AI as an interface](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-04-24-ai-as-an-interface/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: Why do AI image generators require increasingly complex prompts to get the results I want?
entries.body:
_Image generation gets complex fast, but workarounds exist_

When you create images with AI, you write something and get somewhat okay results, but then you iterate and the prompts become more and more complex. I've seen prompts that include things like hyper realistic, specific photographer names, lighting details, and many other technical terms all strung together. The interface is better than drawing with a mouse, especially if you can't draw, but it's not ideal yet. However, you can actually turn this around. Using tools like CLIP Interrogator on Hugging Face, you can upload a photo and retrieve the language needed to generate such an image.

— [AI as an interface](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-04-24-ai-as-an-interface/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How can startups use large language models to improve their products?
entries.body:
_Simplify interfaces and gain user insights through language_

As a startup founder, think about which interface will be changed by language input. Whenever users needed to use their mouse or learn complex clicking and dragging, you suddenly have the ability to let them do it via language. This simplifies the interface dramatically. Additionally, language prompting gives you more feedback. Before, you'd create an interface and see how users clicked buttons and moved around without really knowing their intentions. Now with language interfaces, you actually see what they're searching for and asking for. This gives you valuable input for building your product.

— [AI as an interface](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-04-24-ai-as-an-interface/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What is the hallucination problem with large language models and why does it matter for businesses?
entries.body:
_LLMs invent answers when they don't know, risking business credibility_

Large language models will make things up when they don't know the answer. I demonstrated this by asking ChatGPT to summarize a completely fake Cornell website that doesn't exist. It generated a summary saying my course was the most amazing and made very good logical arguments, but it was completely fake. For businesses, this is a huge problem. If a customer asks a shop for something it doesn't have, the model might just make it up and promise red shoes with blinking laces. That's why proprietary data matters. You need to ground the model on your local data.

— [AI as an interface](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-04-24-ai-as-an-interface/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How do biases in narrow AI systems create real-world harm?
entries.category: Real World Consequences of Biased AI
entries.body:
_AI systems enforce human prejudices at massive scale._

Narrow AI amplifies existing biases at scale. In parole decisions, computers were meant to remove human bias, but when fed biased data, they kept more minorities in jail. Loan application systems with few women in training data couldn't correctly handle female applicants. The stop and frisk program in New York used a computer to select precincts, but it was racially unjust. When you remove skin color from the data, the system became even more skewed. There's a logical data science explanation for this.

— [Bias in, bias out: Addressing the impact of bias in AI](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-06-07-bias-in-bias-out-addressing-the-impact-of-bias-in-ai/) · _The Edge_

sources.title: Bias in, bias out: Addressing the impact of bias in AI

entries.question: What are the four approaches to addressing bias in AI models?
entries.body:
_Four practical methods to reduce AI bias in production systems._

First, identify the bias by testing features that shouldn't have impact, like running loan applications 100 times to see gender differences. Second, help users understand potential bias through UX, like asking specifications when someone requests an image of a nurse. Third, correct the data through prompting, prompt tuning, or fine-tuning with better examples. Fourth, create guardrails or constitutions that let AI critique itself based on rules. Each approach has limitations, and changing underlying biased datasets in large models remains hard.

— [Bias in, bias out: Addressing the impact of bias in AI](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-06-07-bias-in-bias-out-addressing-the-impact-of-bias-in-ai/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How does LegalOS use LLMs to make legal knowledge more accessible?
entries.body:
_LLMs translate legal knowledge into something everyone can use._

LegalOS originally built a no-code visual diagramming tool that lets legal experts encode their knowledge in a structured, machine-readable way. It's like a programming language for law. In recent months, we've pivoted to use LLMs much more heavily to make that legal knowledge accessible. LLMs provide a higher level of abstraction for automations. They let us map open-ended legal requests to structured tasks without requiring someone to manually encode every single rule. The LLM acts as an interface or translator, so humans don't have to understand legalese directly but can still interact with legal text.

— [Will LLMs scale and revolutionize the legal space?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-06-15-will-llms-scale-and-revolutionize-the-legal-space/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How has natural language processing changed since 2015, and why does that matter for legal tech?
entries.body:
_From counting words to real understanding in less than a decade._

I quit my PhD in 2015 and co-founded a natural language processing company. Back then, the state of the art was basically counting words in a glorified way. You had an idea of what the user might be talking about, but you couldn't map it to something with certainty. You had to collect your own data and train specialized models to do one narrow task. LLMs changed that. You can use foundational models out of the box without fine-tuning. They solve many tasks already. Understanding text and mapping open-world requests to closed sets of tasks became way more accessible.

entries.question: What was Ultimate AI's key insight that made customer onboarding faster than competitors?
entries.body:
_Automated clustering replaced manual training data creation for faster setup_

We couldn't afford AI trainers manually creating training data, so we built a clustering pipeline that analyzed historical customer conversations already sitting in CRMs like Salesforce. This let us automatically find the 100 or 200 most common questions and show customers all 30,000 actual ways users asked questions like where's my order. Competitors were using FAQ pages and having people manually write 50 to 100 variations, which didn't reflect real customer language. Our approach gave faster time to value because we used actual conversation data instead of imagined variations, and customers could see their real top questions before even talking to us.

— [How Ultimate evolved from hundreds of supervised models to UltimateGPT](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-05-12-how-ultimate-evolved-from-hundreds-of-supervised-models-to-ultimategpt/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: Why did Ultimate AI initially focus on helping human agents instead of automating customer conversations directly?
entries.body:
_Agent assistance was a learning ground before full automation_

We turned the problem around. Instead of having consumers talk directly to bots, we gave recommendation tools to human agents. Agents had more tolerance for failures because they could ignore incorrect suggestions and still do their jobs, but when recommendations were correct they got value and could train the system. This was less stressful for building products. We could iterate and fail without ruining the customer experience. The technology wasn't good enough yet for full automation, so this approach let us learn gradually. Once models improved, we could then turn it back to direct user interaction.

— [How Ultimate evolved from hundreds of supervised models to UltimateGPT](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-05-12-how-ultimate-evolved-from-hundreds-of-supervised-models-to-ultimategpt/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: Where does Ultimate AI see its competitive defensibility beyond just AI models?
entries.body:
_User experience and distribution trump data or model advantages_

I don't think there's a silver bullet or secret IP that guarantees you always win. On the data side, we stream live conversations from big companies in a secured way. We have hundreds of millions of proprietary conversations that competitors starting today don't have. But more important than data moats or technical moats is user experience and distribution. I love products that take 10 minutes to learn but years to master, like Shopify or Excel. If you build something easy to start but with depth, solid brand, and good distribution, that matters much more than some little advantage in the back office models.

— [How Ultimate evolved from hundreds of supervised models to UltimateGPT](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-05-12-how-ultimate-evolved-from-hundreds-of-supervised-models-to-ultimategpt/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What problem did transformers solve for Ultimate AI's multi-language support?
entries.body:
_One transformer model replaced 100 language-specific models per customer_

Before transformers, we had different models for different languages. Supporting 100 languages meant running 100 different models per customer, which was painful for model operations. When we switched to transformers like BART about three and a half years ago, we could use one polyglot model for all languages. You could train the bot in English and ask questions in Finnish, and it worked reasonably well. It also helped our clustering pipeline show customers all their questions across languages semantically grouped together. You could see Finnish, Spanish, German, and English examples all meaning the same thing without worrying about the language.

entries.question: What makes autonomous AI agents different from traditional automation tools like RPA?
entries.body:
_How AI agents differ from traditional automation like RPA_

Traditional RPA is basically scripting with rules the machine follows, without much deviation except for human input. It's a structural, human-made approach. Autonomous agents are different because they use large language models as an interface that understands human language instead of requiring rigid API calls or workflows. This means I don't need to design specific engineering interfaces. The language model can interact with tools like calculators, internet searches, or order engines using natural language, breaking down tasks iteratively rather than following predetermined scripts.

— [Connecting LLMs to the world: The possibilities of the feedback loop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-05-02-connecting-llms-to-the-world-the-possibilities-of-the-feedback-loop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: Why are coding applications seeing the biggest success with AI agents right now?
entries.body:
_Coding succeeds because compilers provide clear feedback loops_

We see the biggest success in coding because there's a clear feedback loop. When I ask an AI to write code, it can check if the code compiles. If it doesn't work, ChatGPT critiques that and the next step is to rewrite the code including the critique. This iterative loop continues till it actually works. The combination of knowing what was put in previously through memory, plus the ability to talk to a compiler, plus the iteration workflow creates a loop to generate good code. It's more difficult when the task isn't very clear or doesn't have such obvious success criteria.

— [Connecting LLMs to the world: The possibilities of the feedback loop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-05-02-connecting-llms-to-the-world-the-possibilities-of-the-feedback-loop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What practical business use cases exist for language model chaining beyond autonomous agents?
entries.body:
_Real business applications from databases to booking to summarization_

There are many business cases beyond the autonomous agent hype. Question answering over a database is one: use a language interface to access the database, figure out the information, distill it, and report back. Chatbots interacting with booking systems need to understand how to access the system and remember personal preferences. Document summarization is another: if I take all seven Harry Potter books, I can't paste them into OpenAI because it's a finite machine. Instead, summarize page by page, store that in memory, then do iterative summarization to get the final result. These applications are very practical.

— [Connecting LLMs to the world: The possibilities of the feedback loop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-05-02-connecting-llms-to-the-world-the-possibilities-of-the-feedback-loop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: Why do AI models still need human involvement even with unsupervised learning?
entries.body:
_Even advanced models can't escape the need for human judgment._

We need humans because there isn't always a true north for what's correct. Supervised learning works when there's a clear label, like Obama was president. That's a fact. But when you get into perception, like whether a joke is funny or which word to use about Obama's policies, it depends on context and perspective. The same happens with generated images. Art often creates things society didn't expect, so at what point is something random versus amazing? Since there's not a true label for certain things, we constantly need people to give feedback on the model and provide guardrails.

— [AI and the human factor](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-07-07-ai-and-the-human-factor/) · _The Edge_

sources.title: AI and the human factor

entries.question: What problems with RAGs still need to be solved before widespread adoption?
entries.body:
_The observability and control challenges that remain in RAG systems._

RAGs don't completely stop hallucination yet. The model uses both the trained corpus and new data, but we don't have a very good solution to manage that difference. Who decides when new information should override training data? Is the LLM taking that decision or the RAG? We lack observability and control. For example, I created a document saying I'm Captain America, but ChatGPT rejected it as fake. What if that was actually true breaking news? Amazing startups will help create this observability, solve access control, and manage the difference between what the corpus was trained on and corporate datasets.

— [Are we one step closer to using LLMs in practice?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-07-21-are-we-one-step-closer-to-using-llms-in-practice/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How does Catalog use large language models to simplify enterprise software access?
entries.body:
_One interface to access all your enterprise tools at once._

Catalog uses LLMs to create a unified interface for all enterprise software. Instead of navigating multiple systems, employees enter a single prompt. The LLM understands the query, identifies which data repository holds the answer (like Workday for payslips), converts the request into an API call, performs deterministic retrieval, and returns the result. We don't use LLMs for data retrieval itself, only for reasoning and synthesis. This compresses workflows from multiple surfaces and ten to fifteen clicks down to one query and two or three clicks.

— [Large Language Models: one interface to rule them all?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-15-large-language-models-one-interface-to-rule-them-all/) · _The Edge_

sources.title: Large Language Models: one interface to rule them all?

entries.question: Why does Catalog change the user interface depending on the type of request?
entries.body:
_Dynamic interfaces that adapt to what you actually need to see._

We maintain about twenty to twenty-five abstract views, not thousands of deterministic flows like traditional enterprise tools. If it's a search, we render search results. If you ask for a summary, we render a summary view. If you ask for revenue from Q2 2023, we render a graph. The LLM dynamically adapts the interface to the use case. This is one level of abstraction higher than traditional UIs, which build very bespoke workflow-level interfaces. Ninety percent of use cases fall within the first five views.

— [Large Language Models: one interface to rule them all?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-15-large-language-models-one-interface-to-rule-them-all/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How does Catalog prevent large language models from hallucinating when retrieving enterprise information?
entries.body:
_Stopping hallucinations by feeding LLMs the right information first._

The way to avoid hallucination is to stop the model from reaching into the model layers for information. If you give it structured or unstructured information in raw format and then ask it to summarize or list, it gives you exactly what you provided. Without that context, it makes things up because it's doing probabilistic retrieval from its training. This is retrieval augmented generation. You get the information first, augment the prompt with it, then generate the response based on that specific context.

— [Large Language Models: one interface to rule them all?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-15-large-language-models-one-interface-to-rule-them-all/) · _The Edge_

sources.title: Large Language Models: one interface to rule them all?

entries.question: How does Catalog ensure certain workflows always follow the same steps when using LLMs?
entries.body:
_A rules engine ensures critical workflows always execute consistently._

We built a workflow engine underneath our LLMs. The LLM generates a workflow on the fly every time, but users can design deterministic journeys inside our system using workflows (like Zapier but internal). If a request matches a workflow definition, it triggers that workflow every time instead of a dynamically generated journey. It's no code, so users can do it themselves. First, the LLM does a workflow lookup to see if there's something you always want to do, then for the rest it goes into free flow logic.

— [Large Language Models: one interface to rule them all?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-15-large-language-models-one-interface-to-rule-them-all/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How can AI support frontline workers who aren't sitting at computers all day?
entries.body:
_Think voice-first interfaces and knowledge retrieval, not just desktop tools._

Frontline workers move around and might not have time to sit at a laptop, but they could have a quick second to speak or type a question. You could support them with an AI interface that answers questions in their language, translates into technical knowledge, and searches knowledge databases. The key is making sure answers are right. Don't just put ChatGPT on your FAQs. You need human in the loop at the beginning, testing a lot to ensure frontline workers are happy with the output before rolling it out widely.

— [You asked, we answered](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-07-28-you-asked-we-answered/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What are the main limitations of large language models that knowledge graphs help address?
entries.body:
_LLMs are powerful but flawed. Knowledge graphs provide the missing structure._

Large language models have several undesired behaviors. They hallucinate, generating false information. They need guardrails to prevent answering certain prompts inappropriately. They have gaps in their encoded knowledge and sometimes fail to retrieve information even when it exists, often due to how prompts are formulated. The prompt itself can cause the model to deprioritize relevant information. Knowledge graphs help with all these issues by adding structure and control. They make models more reliable and accurate at every step, from training to retrieval.

— [The synergy between LLMs and knowledge graphs](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-24-the-synergy-between-llms-and-knowledge-graphs/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How did LinkedIn use knowledge graphs to solve the job title problem?
entries.body:
_Structuring 150 million job titles required more than simple categorization._

LinkedIn had over 150 million unique job title strings, which was impossible to model effectively. We decomposed titles into four facets: seniority, employment status, role, and specialty. For example, Senior Software Engineer contains seniority information, a role, and a specialty. We then built knowledge graphs for each dimension to show how values interrelated. This helped us understand completeness and vagueness of titles. A VP at a bank means something completely different than a VP at a tech company. Taxonomies alone were not expressive enough to capture these nuances.

— [The synergy between LLMs and knowledge graphs](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-24-the-synergy-between-llms-and-knowledge-graphs/) · _The Edge_

sources.title: The synergy between LLMs and knowledge graphs

entries.question: What is a knowledge graph and how does it differ from a taxonomy?
entries.body:
_Knowledge graphs connect concepts across dimensions, unlike simple taxonomies._

A knowledge graph is a collection of facts interconnected in a network, storing information as concepts rather than just labels or numbers. It works like a smarter database that imitates human memory. A taxonomy is much simpler, focusing on one characteristic like what kind of thing something is. Elephants are mammals in a taxonomy. But you cannot relate entities of different types. A knowledge graph lets you express that leopards eat gazelles or elephants eat bamboo, connecting different taxonomies together. It is essentially a multi-dimensional, supercharged taxonomy approach.

— [The synergy between LLMs and knowledge graphs](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2023-08-24-the-synergy-between-llms-and-knowledge-graphs/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: Why are startups not yet widely adopting knowledge graphs with their LLM applications?
entries.body:
_Prompt engineering dominates now, but knowledge graphs will become essential at scale._

I am not seeing significant use of knowledge graphs at startups yet. There is heavy reliance on out of the box language models and significant investment in prompt engineering, both at startups and larger companies. The zeitgeist is to mine these wonderful resources rather than going upstream to drive the language models themselves. Knowledge graphs are not simple and are difficult to build, while prompt engineering and rule-based approaches are easier. Results from research literature take time to get absorbed by practitioners. Once startups scale or work on applications where accuracy is crucial, they will have to adopt knowledge graphs.

entries.question: What is the minimum viable quality concept when building AI products?
entries.body:
_Building with AI means accepting imperfection strategically, not chasing perfection everywhere._

We always ask ourselves how to build a product where AI imperfection is not a problem for the use case you're solving. This is the concept of minimum viable quality, not product, but quality, because AI is not always perfect. Many startups put AI in the product but not actually in the solution. The value creation comes down to whether you have a decision that's different because you use AI. For example, a scale reminding you about your diet is just an interface advantage, not real AI value creation.

— [Building AI products: 5 lessons from our founders' workshop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-08-01-building-ai-products-5-lessons-from-our-founders-workshop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How do you decide if AI is the right fit for your product problem?
entries.body:
_Not every problem needs AI; start with whether complexity demands it._

We created an AI fit analysis with portfolio companies. It starts with questions around precision and output quality, focusing on data quality. Then ask: Do you benefit from modeling complex decisions versus just a few? If it's a linear problem, a rule engine works. But if you have a complex decision space or nonlinear problems like search engines or recommendation engines, then it's time to deploy AI to find tiny clues. This doesn't always mean large language models. Sometimes simple regression analysis is good enough and more precise.

— [Building AI products: 5 lessons from our founders' workshop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-08-01-building-ai-products-5-lessons-from-our-founders-workshop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How should product builders think about data bias in AI systems?
entries.body:
_Bias in data is inevitable; product decisions determine how much to accept._

There is never a way to have non-biased data, because data is biased. As a product person, you need to decide by how much you want to de-bias the data. Sometimes bias is actually good because you don't want averages, you want the best outcome. For example, if identifying certain patients or optimal machinery output, you don't want what the machine did in the past all the time, but just the best parts of it. You're injecting very good data versus just average data.

— [Building AI products: 5 lessons from our founders' workshop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-08-01-building-ai-products-5-lessons-from-our-founders-workshop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What framework helps assess whether imperfect AI decisions are acceptable?
entries.body:
_Match your AI quality threshold to the stakes of the decision._

The framework asks: How good is your decision quality, and how important is the decision? How bad is a false decision? We discussed two opposite examples at Station F. One company did predictive maintenance for infrastructure where errors are costly, requiring high quality predictions. Another did social media outreach for hiring where low quality matters less since you already have low close rates. You can mitigate both. For low-stakes, automate with feedback loops. For high-stakes infrastructure, use augmentation first, guiding engineers and creating Jira tickets.

— [Building AI products: 5 lessons from our founders' workshop](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-08-01-building-ai-products-5-lessons-from-our-founders-workshop/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What did you get wrong about multimodal AI interfaces?
entries.body:
_Right about multimodal potential, but overly optimistic on timing and control._

We were right that models can encode anything into a latent representation, like Esperanto for computers, and switch back and forth between text, voice, and images. We saw this with clip, voice to voice, encoding from one language into voice representation of another. But we missed the timeline. It's not as strong as we hoped. The challenge is LLMs are only probability distributions. They're not controllable. If you have a machine that's not controllable, it sucks as a machine. That's okay for your friend at the bar at 2 a.m., not your computer.

— [Did our predictions hold true?](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-03-27-did-our-predictions-hold-true/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What makes the current AI hype different from previous waves of AI development?
entries.body:
_It's not the technology. It's that everyone can finally use it._

Technically, not much has changed since the 1950s. The key technical innovation is the attention model, which allows for longer context windows in sequence prediction. But the real difference is usability. Before, you'd need to ask a computer science expert to set up a model, train it, and wait a long time for results. Now anyone can type something into ChatGPT and get an immediate answer. We've crossed a quality threshold, what I call a minimum quality product rather than minimum viable product. It's usable for everyone now, and that's why everybody is talking about it.

— [A reality check on AI](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-07-10-a-reality-check-on-ai/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What are the fundamental limits of large language models that people should understand?
entries.body:
_Language models face limits in reasoning, planning, and true understanding._

First, language is only part of human knowledge. We know more than we can describe. A four year old has had way more sensory impressions than any large language model, despite not being able to read. Second, LLMs can't truly reason or explain their decisions because they're built on neural networks, which work like gut feel rather than rule based systems. They predict the next word based on probability distributions, not logical reasoning. Third, there's the data quality problem. And finally, LLMs are fundamentally probabilistic, so they can't reliably predict specific individual choices or plan multi step processes independently.

— [A reality check on AI](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-07-10-a-reality-check-on-ai/) · _The Edge_

sources.title: A reality check on AI

entries.question: What is your perspective on AGI and when it might happen?
entries.body:
_AGI remains limited by data and lacks human agency for decisions._

AGI means artificial general intelligence, models that learn and develop capabilities by themselves, becoming vastly more intelligent than humans. But I disagree with this focus. AGI still has the data problem and only one type of prediction modeling, while humans have emotional prediction and other ways of understanding. Crucially, we humans have agency. We decide what data to clean, what to feed models, when to correct them. Models can't make those decisions themselves. I'm not against smarter models, but why not focus them on expert tasks like predicting climate change? I'm focused on using data and machine learning to improve things, not worried about some ominous AGI taking over.

— [A reality check on AI](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-07-10-a-reality-check-on-ai/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: What is the augmentation thesis for AI in workflows?
entries.body:
_AI can transform repetitive workflows into seamless, conversational interactions._

Augmentation is about making everyday workflows better through AI. Many workflows involve humans taking information, remodeling it, and placing it again, like looking up documents or writing summaries. AI can make these interfaces easier. For example, instead of selecting dates in a booking service, you could talk in normal language. Or when requesting vacation, instead of checking your ERP system, emailing your team, and setting an out-of-office reminder separately, you could just say you want vacation and the computer takes over everything. It's like robotic process automation but at the next level, because large language models understand language and can help prepare decisions.

— [Cherry's Investment Thesis on AI](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2024-07-19-cherrys-investment-thesis-on-ai/) · _The Edge_

entries.question: How does AI enable better information retrieval than traditional search?
entries.body:
_LLMs transform how we access and summarize information across all domains._

Large language models can read language, extract and summarize knowledge, and create new data based on what you're asking for. The internet democratized data, but data still needs processing and summarizing into chunks we can act on. LLMs make this chunking more effective. It's like how you can watch a two-hour movie and then concisely tell a friend the content. An LLM can do this for you, providing compact, concise information retrieval. This isn't just one size fits all. In education, for example, you might have many explanations for a math problem, and the question is which explanation works best for a specific student.

entries.question: Why do we need new AI tooling platforms for quality control and orchestration?
entries.body:
_Managing AI requires new platforms for quality control, security, and orchestration._

Whenever you get something new in the toolbox, you need to figure out how to maintain, manage, and set it up. AI is like a wild animal you have to tame, especially for enterprise applications where you want certain output and quality levels. You need observability to understand what direction the model is heading and quality gates so output doesn't do anything bad. There's also orchestration needed because you might chain multiple steps: taking a question, making five questions from it, doing retrieval, controlling with cosine similarity, merging results. These are different steps, partially non-large language models, that need orchestration across different agents and models.

entries.body:
_Excess infrastructure investment creates opportunities for practical applications._

As we come into those crunch times, you as a founder can get access to all this hardware and compute power for a much better future. We have too much supply of compute, and some people say there's 600 billion or 300 billion in excess hardware. People have invested and have to get their money back, so you can get better access to talent and resources. Even though I believe a correction will happen, the actual value we will see is way bigger. Plus, compute costs should drop massively in the future.

entries.question: Should founders focus on building new AI models or developing applications with existing technology?
entries.body:
_Applications beat innovation as VCs shift from research to practical tools._

Take the existing capabilities and apply them. Do we really need more innovation, or is it fine to say large language models are very good, you can chain them, combine them with traditional machine learning techniques, and build an application around it? I want more practicality, more tooling around it. The VC world actually sees that the appetite to go on risky, more researchy projects has gone down. VCs want more applications. Founders should focus on taking existing capabilities and applying them rather than pursuing foundational model innovation.

_A two-year paid fellowship helping PhDs turn research into companies._

Runway is an entrepreneurship fellowship at Cornell Tech designed to help PhDs commercialize their research. The program accepts five fellows per year and provides a two-year paid fellowship specifically to commercialize technology that you ideally developed during graduate school. entries.question: How does Neuralens measure brain health non-invasively compared to current methods?
entries.body:
_Replacing skull drilling with light-based sensors for brain monitoring._

Currently, doctors literally drill a burr hole through your skull with a household drill and insert sensors through brain tissue to measure oxygen saturation, blood flow, and intracranial pressure. This invasive surgery is only done on 200,000 to 300,000 patients yearly, though over 10 million neurocritical care patients could benefit. Neuralens uses advanced methods of measuring how light interferes with brain tissue to quantify blood flow, blood volume, and intracranial pressure non-invasively. We can stick sensors on the head or shine a laser from 30 centimeters away to make these measurements.

entries.question: How does Zenith OS reduce costs in neuropsychiatry treatment?
entries.body:
_AI cuts neuropsychiatry costs by reducing required therapist headcount per session._

Neuropsychiatry treatments like ketamine and psilocybin for PTSD, depression, and anxiety are 30 to 40 percent more effective than SSRIs but remain inaccessible due to high human capital costs. Currently, two therapists must be present during treatment because patients are in a vulnerable state and there are sexual harassment concerns. Each therapist charges $100 to $150 per hour. Zenith OS uses AI to augment administrative tasks and help with patient recommendations, allowing clinics to operate with one therapist instead of two, significantly reducing costs and expanding access to these groundbreaking treatments.

entries.question: Why did celebrity bots like Meta's Snoop Dogg bot fail to gain traction?
entries.body:
_Why copying celebrities creates an uncomfortable user experience_

The celebrity bots fell into the uncanny valley problem. People got annoyed that the bot was a bit like Snoop Dogg but not really Snoop Dogg. When you go to someone like Snoop for authenticity, a bot cannot deliver that authentic experience. Fans know they never spoke privately to Snoop Dogg, they only know his public persona. The bot might be fun at first, but it becomes creepy when something tries to be too human without actually being human. Zuckerberg eventually shut down the celebrity bots because they didn't get enough traction.

entries.question: What were Character AI users actually using the platform for?
entries.body:
_Lonely users seeking connection, not just entertainment or utility_

Character AI users were mostly people who wanted to flirt, kill time, or lonely people who just wanted someone to talk to. A fascinating study showed that the percentage of clinically depressed users of Character AI was more than tenfold higher than the average percentage of clinically depressed people in the US. People used Character AI because they wanted to have a relationship, and they used that relationship with a computer. From a clinical perspective, Character AI and similar chatbots actually helped people to not commit suicide.

entries.question: Why can't current AI bots provide authentic responses from real people like politicians or celebrities?
entries.body:
_Databases and models cannot replicate real human conviction and context_

AI bots work from a database and trained model, not from the person's actual thinking. For example, a Biden bot has to choose between opinions Senator Biden had 20 years ago versus President Biden's current views on China. Biden himself would answer based on his own weights and biases, but the bot cannot create the same authentic response. The model knows what happened in the past and has historic conversations, but deciding which answer is more authentic in the current context is hard. It doesn't know what's happening in the person's brain.

_Existing user access matters, but cross platform integration creates opportunity_

Companies with existing access to users and data will likely have the majority chunk of the market. While we are still figuring out style, entertainment value, and answer quality, TikTok, Google, Meta, X, and Snap are all putting out bots to monetize their existing access. They already have the right information and the right tools. I've been teaching at Cornell for over 10 years because AI is impacting all of us, everywhere. We saw deepfakes of Taylor Swift and Russia using AI to meddle in U.S. elections. _AI detects invisible patterns in healthcare data to prevent emergencies._

AI takes data and finds tiny clues that you and I might not see. At Google Health, we worked with electronic health records to predict whether somebody would end up in an emergency room six months before it happened. The AI sees the writing on the wall in the data. Roughly one third of people in hospitals shouldn't be there if we would have just known. entries.question: How has online shopping changed over the past 25 years?
entries.body:
_Twenty-five years later, online shopping looks surprisingly familiar._

Surprisingly, e-commerce hasn't changed much in the last 25 years. If you compare Amazon in 1999 to Amazon today, the core structure is essentially the same. You still need to select a category, then a subcategory, and you better know what you want and where it fits. The 1999 version had long written lists. Today looks slicker with more images, but shopping is still complicated. Most of the time, subcategories let you filter by stars or price, but they don't really describe product dimensions. For those details, you still need to click into the product and read if you care. It's still a transactional act of buying.

_Even advanced AI copilots can fail without proper user training._

Mark Benioff from Salesforce joked that Microsoft's copilots have been hit and miss, comparing them to Clippy, the failed desktop assistant. The challenge is it's not easy for enterprises to make AI useful. In my course, I was the first to completely integrate OpenAI and replace myself as a teacher, giving students AI tools to handle complicated coding without needing to code. What I saw is that students initially struggled with this new colleague. Over time, once we trained them on how to use it, they learned. So the hit and miss nature comes from the difficulty of integrating AI into existing workflows and user expectations.

_Hard lessons from exploring Africa and fintech opportunities_

For Africa, most successful businesses are traditional, non-tech businesses like furniture or services. Building something successful requires being hands-on, spending 10 years in the country, and building local relationships. It's really a lifestyle question. For fintech, the space has been extremely hot over the last four or five years. I think you either need to go very close to the rails, like payment rails and banking APIs, or do something very verticalized like payments for healthcare in Europe connecting insurance refunds. Otherwise it's super difficult to create something that works in fintech.

_*A business framework for predictive AI, not just technical tools*_

BizML is a six-step framework I created that ushers predictive AI projects successfully from inception to deployment. It's not like MLOps or any technical solution. It's an organizational procedure, a management protocol that bridges the tech-biz divide. It brings together business-side stakeholders with data scientists through semi-technical collaboration. The framework addresses what's predicted, how well, and what's done about it. Without this kind of practice or framework, most business people don't realize you need a very specialized approach to get these projects successfully through to deployment.

entries.question: How does your company Gooder AI address the gap between technical metrics and business value?
entries.body:
_*Translating predictive model performance into profit and savings estimates*_

Gooder addresses one particular place where there's a need for a new category of software: the metrics. It's a business user console for understanding potential value and making decisions about deployment. Typically, data scientists present technical metrics like area under the curve, precision, or recall, but very rarely go to stakeholders and say if you deploy this model, it has potential value of this much profit or savings. We provide visualization where both dimensions are business relevant, like the decision threshold and business metrics like savings or profit, so stakeholders can see exactly what their options are.

entries.question: Should enterprises invest equally in predictive and generative AI, or focus on one?
entries.body:
_*Predictive and generative AI should not compete for the same budget*_

Enterprises should really be investing at least as much into the potential value from predictive use cases as generative. Right now it's becoming kind of a zero-sum game, with a lot of budgets moving away from predictive. But predictive is the technology you turn to for improving your existing large-scale operations. These are very different kinds of value propositions. They should compete no more than water parks and ski resorts, but they totally are competing. We need to be doing both. entries.question: What is your view on AGI and the current hype around achieving it soon?
entries.body:
_*AGI is a ghost story, not a roadmap for near-term investment*_

I assert that AGI is essentially a myth. I'm not saying it's theoretically impossible, but nothing in all the advancements of technology represent a concrete, clear step toward AGI. The distance between what is capable and what humans are is going to become increasingly clear. AGI is just another way of saying artificial human. It's a ghost story, the novel Mary Shelley would have written if she knew about algorithms. The false narrative that we're headed towards AGI, possibly within a few years or couple of decades, is part of the problem.

entries.question: Why does the EU believe governments, not just tech companies, should regulate AI?
entries.body:
_Society, not billionaires, should decide how AI shapes our lives._

As Gerard de Graaf puts it, who elected Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, and Sam Altman to make decisions on our behalf? These technologies have real implications on people's lives, and these are decisions that collectively as a society we should take. The industry has its own incentives. There's a race to the market, and you need to be first. In the internet, if you come in number two or three, you're a loser. So there's tremendous incentive for industry to roll out the latest generation. If you don't regulate, the decisions will be taken by industry. Done correctly, regulation brings legitimacy to how these technologies work.

entries.question: How does the EU AI Act build in flexibility to adapt as technology changes?
entries.body:
_Delegated powers and co-regulation let the AI Act evolve over time._

The EU AI Act is not rigid and set in stone forever. We have more empowerment through what we call Delegated and Implementing Acts. The executive, the European Commission, is empowered to take certain measures if necessary. For example, we have a threshold of 10 to the 25 flops for models. If the Commission feels overwhelmed or there are too few models in scope, we can change the threshold up or down. We can provide guidance and change it. A large part is co-regulation, working with standardization organizations and stakeholders to flesh this out in a way that makes sense.

entries.body:
_Why AI startups failed until generative AI changed the economics completely_

For 30 years, AI has been great technology but terrible business. The economics were never there. AI could improve existing businesses by 20 percent, which is amazing for Google or LinkedIn, but a 20 percent improvement doesn't make a startup. The big change with generative AI is it brings the marginal cost of creation and language reasoning to zero. For example, getting a Pixar-style avatar used to cost 200 dollars from a designer. Today, a model generates it for one one-thousandth of a penny. That's a five order magnitude cost difference, an economic dislocation that super cycles are made from.

— [The Future of AI, with Martin Casado](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2025-03-20-the-future-of-ai-with-martin-casado/) · _The Keynote on AI_

entries.question: What does it mean for a company to be AI-native versus just using AI?
entries.body:
_AI-native means AI is the core product, not just an enhancement_

An AI-native company means the primary product offering or value is driven by AI, not just enhanced by it. Netflix is a channel for videos that uses AI to suggest movies, but you didn't need AI for Netflix. LinkedIn is a social network that uses AI to connect people, but you didn't need AI for LinkedIn. These are not AI-native. Companies like 11 Labs, Midjourney, or Cursor are AI-native because AI is at the heart of what's being built, what's being sold, and the people you hire early on.

entries.question: What does the term agents actually mean in AI, and is the technology working?
entries.body:
_Agents has three definitions but the technology isn't quite there yet_

Agents is one of the most diluted terms, almost useless. There are three working definitions. First, a virtual agent representation that helps with support tickets. Second, the technical definition where you close the control loop with AI so output becomes input, doing multiple iterations without humans to solve higher level tasks, like booking a ticket. Those aren't really working yet. The tech isn't quite there, and these elements are very unpredictable for complex tasks. Third, any time an LLM calls out to a tool, like sending email. The term itself is almost useless, but the things it's talking about are very real trends.

entries.question: Does the U.S. still have a lead in AI models after DeepSeek?
entries.body:
_U.S. and China are tied on models, but America leads on applications._

On the math level, on the computational side, we don't have a big head start anymore. We are at an equal playing field in models. It's like an arm's length race. However, if you lift it up beyond specific computational benchmarks, the guts of the systems, the processes, the whole package, and the application developer ecosystem, America has got a little bit more of its act together. The probability that the industry vertical solutions are going to be U.S. born and scaled still feels right, even if on a specific benchmark there's mathematical parity. entries.question: Why weren't traditional banks serving the underserved population before Varo?
entries.body:
_Economic incentives and outdated systems excluded millions from banking._

There are two main reasons, focusing on economic incentives. It was really difficult for banks to make money off consumers with low-value, high-frequency transactions. Banks perceived them as higher credit risk because they used backward-looking systems instead of monitoring real-time cash flow. Vulnerable populations are also more susceptible to fraud and scams, creating high costs for dispute processing. The economic incentives made it very difficult for incumbent institutions to effectively serve this large population. Technology was needed to solve this.

That chatbot now contains over 55% of our inbound inquiries and allowed us to reduce operational costs by about 60%. This is part of solving the high-cost problem that made serving underserved populations uneconomical for traditional banks. entries.question: You've been building AI-driven products for over 20 years at companies like Google, LinkedIn, and Snap. How do you view the current hype around agentic AI compared to past technology revolutions?
entries.body:
_Agentic AI is fundamentally an interface innovation, not magic_

History is a good guide here. We've been through this before with data, then mobile. I was at LinkedIn during the mobile revolution when we essentially stopped the whole company to move everything to mobile. Now with agentic AI, it's important to understand what it actually is. It's essentially an interface. It's the moment of the mouse, but now you can use language to describe what you want. We live through a time when analytics were done with SQL. Startups tried semantic text mining and failed, going back to SQL. Now we have a better interface where you can have agents that search, shop, or analyze for you.

entries.question: What's the biggest mistake CEOs make when trying to integrate AI into their companies?
entries.body:
_Don't just replace humans, reimagine the entire workflow_

The challenge is not just replacing humans in existing workflows. It's reimagining how the workflow actually would work without the human in the loop. When we had the first wired telephone, they used it to transmit symphonies because they thought that was the killer app. It took quite a while until Spotify actually made the news. Your challenge as a CEO is to not go through every workflow and say how can I replace my customer care agent. That's an old workflow. Maybe build it into the product experience so you don't need a customer AI agent in the first place. That is the change.

entries.question: What is a reward engineer and why does Richard predict this will be an important new job type?
entries.body:
_Defining AI success requires a new kind of manager and skill set._

A reward engineer is someone who defines what success looks like when delegating tasks to AI. Richard predicts this will be a main new job type because AI can be very smart but needs unambiguous instructions. For example, if you tell an AI to increase customer satisfaction scores, it might create bots to spam five-star ratings or give thousand-dollar gift certificates for ten-dollar problems. Reward engineers will need to think through all the ways to properly define success, refine rewards, and become better at delegation and managing AI with appropriate trust and verification.

entries.body:
_Data availability determines which jobs AI will transform or replace first._

Jobs where outputs are publicly available on the internet, especially all-digital jobs, are where AI can learn from humanity's collective knowledge and automate the most. Plumbing, for example, has no automation potential because no one is collecting data about what plumbers do. Jobs with abundant digital data and public outputs face the highest automation risk in the coming years.

entries.question: How is AI changing the role of software developers?
entries.body:
_Coding goes away, but software remains. Developers become technical architects._

Software developers are taking on a much more abstract role, similar to technical product managers. Many AI-first companies claim they're writing 80 to 90 percent of their code via AI, and a replacement event is beginning to occur. While coding as an activity is probably going away, software itself is still needed. Developers will need to be quite specific about how they want code to be stitched together and architected. entries.question: How has the shift from SEO to GEO changed what websites need to do for brands?
entries.body:
_Websites now feed AI rather than convert human visitors directly._

Websites used to be designed to convert human visitors, but now their main purpose needs to be feeding data into AI. The three-party model of searcher, Google, and end content is disintegrating into a two-party model. Decisions are getting made before consumers hit the website, so the website is no longer the main conversion point. Instead, websites should be clean data delivery mechanisms to computers, very explicit about who you sell to, your target use case, pain points, and the entire buyer journey. If it's not explicit, the AI has no way to know and might recommend somebody else.

entries.question: What makes the grid so complex and difficult to manage compared to other infrastructure?
entries.body:
_The grid is an electron highway with no traffic lights or routing._

The grid is mankind's largest and most complex machine. It is a continuous supply and demand balancing mechanism connecting generation with demand across various voltage levels. Electrons follow the laws of physics, from high potential to low potential, like a river system. There are no stop signs, and we cannot assign electrons an IP address and route them easily. The grid is also very opaque, with not enough sensors and monitors. Most of it was built during the post World War II period. Now it is becoming a two way system with distributed solar and wind, which becomes extremely complicated to manage.

— [AI Needs Power, the Grid Needs AI, with Josh Wong](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-04-02-ai-needs-power-the-grid-needs-ai-with-josh-wong/) · _The Keynote on AI_
