entries.question: How does Think Labs AI use physics informed AI differently than general purpose models like ChatGPT?
entries.body:
_Grid AI must be grounded in physics, not just patterns in data._

We cannot just put SCADA measurements and smart metering information into ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot or Gemini and ask how the grid works. It does not work like that. We lean into something called Physics Informed AI. We train our AI models using physics. It is physics driven, physics based, and physics accurate. We teach AI how the grid works and reproduce engineering analysis faithfully. The AI can turn traditional studies that take weeks to months into minutes, and go from analyzing one feeder at a time into full system analysis.

— [AI Needs Power, the Grid Needs AI, with Josh Wong](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-04-02-ai-needs-power-the-grid-needs-ai-with-josh-wong/) · _The Keynote on AI_

entries.body:
_You remain accountable for your AI agents, like a CEO for employees._

If people write an email and that email is wrong, who is accountable for it? Should I say it was my AI agent? Not quite. It was me who trained and set up and focused an AI agent. We talk about the new role that all of us become managers or CEOs of many agents. If that description is true, then the accountability lies in you, the CEO. entries.question: What does true swarming mean, and how is it different from choreography?
entries.body:
_Real swarms have no leader; each drone decides independently._

Some companies have drones flying in formation or following a leader, self-healing formations that rearrange when members are shut down. I consider that choreography, not actual swarming. True swarming means every single member of the group knows everything about all the other members and makes its own independent decisions. There is no leader, no single point of failure. They all know the objectives and negotiate among themselves who does what to achieve it. It is a swarm where they are all equal partners, just with different capabilities.

entries.question: How does jamming affect drone operations, and why does it make autonomy necessary?
entries.body:
_Communication denial forces drones to decide without waiting for human orders._

Jammers emit white noise across frequencies to drown out communication. GPS satellite signals go first because they are weak. Your connection to home base gets jammed second because you are far away and the jammer is closer. But drones close together, only hundreds of meters apart, can still communicate with each other because the nearest jammer is kilometers away. You have to assume information from home base arrives intermittently at best. This is why drones must make autonomous decisions. They cannot wait for human instructions that may never arrive.

— [AI on the Front Lines, with Alexander Fink](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-04-30-ai-on-the-front-lines-with-alexander-fink/) · _The Keynote on AI_

entries.question: What level of autonomy does Swarmar allow in target engagement, and where do humans decide?
entries.body:
_Humans mark targets; drones autonomously track and engage them._

Humans decide what needs to be done. They set the mission, the targets, the rules of engagement, when to abort, and what to do in every fallback scenario. Once drones launch, they execute according to what humans decided. In our seek and hit missions, surveillance drones find targets and send video to the operator. The operator marks the target. Then terminal guidance and tracking while attack drones are incoming is done autonomously by the drones themselves. The human decision was the thing at these coordinates at this timestamp is your target.

entries.question: What did Ben learn at LinkedIn about predicting company success with data?

entries.body:
_Only founder data predicts early stage success, not company metrics._

Working with the data science team at LinkedIn, we evaluated whether there are signals in the data to predict future company success. After series B, there are signals. Market signals and signals internal to LinkedIn data are predictive. Things like the quality of where you're hiring from, how many people you win compared to how many you lose to other companies. entries.question: What is the most important format for presenting dealership content to AI models?
entries.body:
_Q&A format reduces cognitive load and increases AI model pickup._

Package your content in Q&A format. When someone asks a question, the model looks for the least cognitive load, very much like humans. If it finds the exact question already formatted with an answer, it just picks that up rather than reading a sentence and having to think about extracting the answer. That costs money for the model. So take your newsletters from the last 10 years, use an AI tool to generate Q&As from that authentic content, and put it on your website. The content should be human generated, ideally based on your own customer data.

entries.question: Why shouldn't dealerships use ChatGPT or other AI tools to create content for GEO?
entries.body:
_AI-generated content harms your visibility in generative search results._

Do not ask ChatGPT, Gemini, or other tools to create content for you. It will not work. All model providers are extremely careful about trying to figure out slop, which is AI-generated content. The model doesn't learn from content it just created. This is the snake eating its own tail. If you create slop, you will lose out. Use your human team to bring content in. Your content needs to be authentic, novel, and unique. You can use AI tools to help organize your authentic content, like generating Q&As from your existing newsletters, but not to create the original content.

entries.question: How did you use quizzes to improve the flipped classroom model?
entries.body:
_Quizzes revealed where students struggled before class even started._

I asked students to do a quiz before coming to class to find out which areas they didn't understand. For example, a FiveThirtyEight video on k-means clustering Margaritas was fun, but the quiz revealed it failed to explain where the 'k' in k-means came from. This feedback let me spend more time on that point in class than I would have usually done. Content curation became the critical path, and quizzes helped me identify gaps.

entries.question: What engagement methods did you test and which worked best?

_Student surveys revealed multiple-choice questionnaires won for engagement._

I experimented with cold-calling via a random number generator, multiple-choice questionnaires, discussions in smaller groups, and other methods. After surveying students after each class, multiple-choice questionnaires came out on top. I created them for every 10 minutes of my course to ensure my speed was right and measure my teaching performance. I also used a Google Spreadsheet where students outlined answers in one to two sentences, then picked the most interesting ones to discuss.

entries.body:
_Pre-screening answers leveled the playing field for introverts and extroverts._

Traditional classrooms favored extroverts, but pre-screening answers and quizzes let everyone participate. I used multiple-choice questionnaires and a Google Spreadsheet where students outlined discussion answers in one to two sentences. I could follow live and pick the most interesting answers to discuss in class. This pre-screening of arguments worked extremely well to create robust class discussion outcomes, giving all students a voice regardless of personality type.

I also spiced up the course with fun actions using Snap Cam to change myself into a potato or come in a Tuxedo to class. entries.question: Why didn't MOOCs revolutionize education as predicted in 2012?
entries.body:
_Traditional classrooms remained more adaptive than early online learning platforms._

Universities have high fixed costs, and online so far offered only minimal marginal revenue. More importantly, a traditional classroom was more adaptive than MOOCs. entries.question: What is the difference between AGI, singularity, and superintelligence?
entries.body:
_Understanding the core terms of the AGI conversation today_

AGI, or artificial general intelligence, is the ability to generalize beyond what you were trained for. If given an unfamiliar environment and goal, it should figure out how to achieve that goal through creative imagination and trial and error. Singularity, coined by Vernor Vinge and popularized by Ray Kurzweil, refers to a point where the rate of progress feels infinite to legacy humans. This happens through recursive self-improvement, where an AI makes a smarter AI. Superintelligence follows AGI. Many believe that once we achieve human-level AGI, it will optimize its own code and exceed human levels much faster than predicted, creating a steep exponential curve rather than gradual progress.

— [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-05-28-rethinking-the-agi-race-with-benjamin-goertzel/) · _The Keynote on AI_

entries.question: Why are current large language models not considered true AGI?
entries.body:
_Catastrophic forgetting and frozen weights limit today's LLMs_

LLMs have significant limitations that prevent them from being AGI. First, they suffer from catastrophic forgetting because learning and inference are separate phases. The weights freeze after training, so the system cannot continuously learn in real time. Second, they store knowledge more like a huge catalog of special cases rather than true abstraction. Third, they do not reorganize themselves in context of real-time interactions the way human brains do. While LLMs can do impressive things like math proofs and reasoning about novel scenarios, they lack the kind of generalizable, self-integrating knowledge system needed for AGI. They are more like an off-ramp on the path to AGI.

— [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-05-28-rethinking-the-agi-race-with-benjamin-goertzel/) · _The Keynote on AI_

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel

entries.question: Why do major tech CEOs keep claiming AGI is imminent when current AI still has obvious limitations?
entries.body:
_Market pressures shape how companies talk about AGI timelines publicly_

There is tension between AGI timelines and current product reality. While Altman, Musk, and Hassabis suggest AGI is near or already here, anyone who codes knows current systems still fail frequently. At Google I/O, Demis Hassabis mentioned AGI by 2029 and being at the foothills of singularity, but this was buried at the end. Most of the keynote focused on incremental AI features in products. This makes sense because publicly listed companies need to highlight quarterly profits. Saying AGI comes in 2029 might cause investors to dump stock and wait. So companies focus on near-term utility while their research arms pursue AGI separately. The timeline itself has become more plausible to many, though skeptics remain.

— [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-05-28-rethinking-the-agi-race-with-benjamin-goertzel/) · _The Keynote on AI_

sources.title: Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel

entries.question: What makes achieving general intelligence fundamentally different from doing many specialized tasks well?
entries.body:
_Generalization beyond training data defines AGI, not task breadth alone_

The key difference is the learning and generalization capability, not breadth of tasks. A system that does 95% of human jobs by copying millions of training examples is not AGI, even if economically valuable. True AGI must take a leap beyond what it was prepared for and generalize from what it knows to do new things. If you describe a novel alien civilization with bizarre customs never in training data, and the system reasons about it from multiple perspectives, that shows real inductive and abductive reasoning. AGI should figure out how to achieve unfamiliar goals in unfamiliar environments through creative imagination and trial and error, not just pattern matching against a massive catalog of prior examples.

— [Rethinking the AGI Race, with Benjamin Goertzel](https://www.lutzfinger.com/transcript/2026-05-28-rethinking-the-agi-race-with-benjamin-goertzel/) · _The Keynote on AI_

entries.question: Why don't people trust Facebook with their data anymore?
entries.body:
_Trust erodes when data sharing is careless and opaque._

We don't trust Facebook anymore because we learned that they gave away our data way too carelessly. The real issue isn't about who has access to our data, but rather what the data is actually used for. Since we don't know what happens with our data once Facebook has it, trust has eroded. The outcry over WhatsApp's updated privacy policy, which disclosed data sharing with Facebook, reflects this deeper mistrust. It doesn't matter what Facebook does at this point because the trust is already broken.

entries.question: What kinds of personal characteristics can be predicted from Facebook data?
entries.body:
_Facebook data reveals far more about us than we realize._

Michal Kosinski showed in 2013 that using Facebook data could accurately predict sexual orientation, ethnicity, personality traits, intelligence, happiness, addictive substances use, parental separation, age, and gender. The model even managed to separate between Democrat and Republican in 85% of cases. This research demonstrates how powerful social media data can be for profiling individuals, which contributes to why people feel uncomfortable when they don't know how their data is being used without their knowledge.

— [WhatsApp: We Should Discuss What Our Data Is Used For, Not Who Has It](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2021/01/26/whatsapp-we-should-discuss-what-our-data-is-used-for-not-who-has-it/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: How did we learn that location data from our phones was being sold?
entries.body:
_Pandemic dashboards exposed a hidden ecosystem of location tracking._

During the pandemic, many companies created dashboards showing aggregated movement data. This revealed that smaller companies like Unacast and Placer.ai gathered location information via hundreds of apps on your phone. Additionally, phone companies Sprint, AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon sold our location data. There is an entire ecosystem of apps that share a lot of information about us. WhatsApp is probably not the biggest privacy offender we have in our phones when you consider this broader data sharing landscape.

entries.question: What example shows how data use in one industry could be inappropriate in another?
entries.body:
_Healthcare data belongs with doctors, not insurance pricing algorithms._

In healthcare, we want doctors to use health data to diagnose our potential issues. But we do not expect our doctor to share health information with an insurance company that will then change the pricing of our life insurance. The healthcare industry is regulated to prevent this kind of misuse. However, the social media industry is not similarly regulated. This example illustrates why we should focus on what data is used for, not just who has it, and why regulation matters.

entries.question: How might data regulation affect innovation and global competition?
entries.body:
_Regulation may slow innovation but remains necessary for trust._

Regulation of data use will force companies to ask for consent before developing new algorithms. This extra step will inadvertently slow down innovation and might be a factor in the global innovation competition. China can correlate and analyze datasets without regulatory constraints, creating a competitive advantage. Despite this challenge, we need to regulate our markets and expect international partners to comply with the same rules. We should push for clear regulations and international norms on transparency, accountability, and data ownership.

entries.question: What are the three main problems with training data that can cause AI to get things wrong?
entries.body:
_Three critical failures that undermine machine learning accuracy and fairness._

Training data can fail in three ways. First, it might not be sufficient. The data may lack context or situations the algorithm will encounter in the real world. Second, it might be biased. This means data is systematically missing certain perspectives or groups. For example, if texts predominantly show nurses as women, the algorithm learns that pattern without understanding societal goals like gender equality. Third, the data might be outright wrong. Labels may be inaccurate or based on performances rather than reality, leading algorithms to learn incorrect associations.

— [It's The Data, Stupid! Why AI Might Get It Wrong.](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2020/05/28/its-the-data-stupid-why-ai-might-get-it-wrong/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: How did the Apple Card algorithm discriminate despite not using gender as a direct feature?
entries.body:
_Apple Card offered vastly different limits to spouses with identical assets._

David Heinemeier Hansson was offered a credit limit 20 times higher than his wife despite having the same shared assets. The algorithm likely learned from a world where men earn on average more than women and concluded that men are more creditworthy. This shows how bias creeps in even when protected characteristics like gender aren't direct features. The training data itself was biased, reflecting existing societal inequalities, and the algorithm learned to perpetuate them without explicitly considering gender.

— [It's The Data, Stupid! Why AI Might Get It Wrong.](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2020/05/28/its-the-data-stupid-why-ai-might-get-it-wrong/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: Why is emotion detection training data problematic, according to the article?
entries.body:
_Algorithms learn performed emotions, not real ones, from limited datasets._

Emotion detection algorithms were often trained on the JAFFE dataset, which contains images of 10 Japanese female models performing seven facial expressions. The problem is the algorithm doesn't learn how someone actually looks when angry, but rather how those specific women performed an angry expression. This distinction is critical. The models were acting out emotions rather than genuinely experiencing them, so the training data captures performance, not authentic emotional states. This makes the foundation of emotion detection fundamentally flawed.

— [It's The Data, Stupid! Why AI Might Get It Wrong.](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2020/05/28/its-the-data-stupid-why-ai-might-get-it-wrong/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What does the article say we need to address AI data problems going forward?
entries.body:
_No quick solutions exist; fairness itself remains hard to define precisely._

There's no easy fix coming. Beyond technical difficulties, researchers struggle with defining what is fair. We need tools to check for biases and missing data in our models. We also need the right incentives to check for drift and update algorithms as society changes. Drift happens when datasets become biased over time even if initially unbiased, because society and beliefs evolve. Machine learning and AI will be powerful forces for good, but only if the training data is correct and fair.

entries.question: Why does Clubhouse's future success depend on using user data?
entries.body:
_Finding content on Clubhouse is hard without better data use._

Clubhouse's future success depends on how it can help users find content and enable engagement through the use of user data. At the core, any social app solves two issues: to find and enable social interactions. Currently, finding interesting conversations on Clubhouse is not easy. You curate your own content by following people, similar to how Twitter used the social graph as a first approximation for your interest. A social graph is a clunky way to curate your feed. In order to scale, Clubhouse will need data and engagement metrics.

entries.question: How does TikTok's algorithm differ from Clubhouse's approach to content discovery?
entries.body:
_TikTok uses behavior and content analysis, not social graphs._

TikTok is an algorithm-first company. Unlike Clubhouse or Facebook, it does not mainly rely on the social graph but has built a powerful recommendation engine. TikTok's machine learning magic is a supervised learning system that finds videos interesting to the user by measuring how long you look, how fast you scroll, and many other behavioral features. Additionally, the algorithm evaluates the actual video clip: content, speed, sound, colors, words. Bytedance has an absurd proportion of their software engineers focused on their algorithms. This data has created a sizable moat that not even Facebook could cross easily.

entries.body:
_Live transcription is technically possible but not currently implemented._

To find the right discussion for you, Clubhouse would need to understand all conversations, meaning it would need to live-transcribe them. Technically this is feasible. Speech to text algorithms have become very powerful. Clubhouse is currently not transcribing conversations, presumably to preserve the authenticity of the moment. However, streaming companies like Spotify or Deezer can tell you that a delay between the user's dislike and an action such as skip makes it harder for the algorithm to work correctly. Clubhouse will need data and engagement metrics to scale.

_Twitter and Facebook have social graphs and content spread measurement._

I expect the fiercest competitors to be Twitter and Facebook, as they bring existing social network graphs and also measure how content spreads. As Clubhouse grows, their design choices will be necessary. Whether or not Clubhouse will become a super-aggregator will depend on their ability to create a multi-sided network with decreasing acquisition costs. entries.body:
_Clubhouse mirrors talk radio but doesn't exploit digital advantages._

Clubhouse is Internet 1.0 of Talk Radio. Ten years before the internet browser was invented, Talk Radio became popular for similar reasons: ease in distribution and proliferation of content. AM Bands allowed for more bandwidth to distribute content. Four decades later, the internet brought the same two effects. entries.question: How did you isolate trust as a factor in COVID vaccination rates?
entries.body:
_Using the EU to study trust's role in vaccination._

We looked towards the EU because the distribution of vaccines to Member States happened simultaneously and under the same conditions. But not all member states show the same trust, allowing us to isolate trust as a variable. We used the European Social Survey, a bi-annually collected survey of thousands of EU citizens from 29 countries, to measure trust levels. We then correlated that data with vaccination data from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.

— [Get Vaccinated? How Trust In Institutions Determines COVID Vaccination Rates In The EU](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2021/05/06/get-vaccinated-how-trust-into-the-institutions-determines-vaccination-rates-in-the-eu/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: Get Vaccinated? How Trust In Institutions Determines COVID Vaccination Rates In The EU

entries.question: What did the data show about high trust versus low trust countries?
entries.body:
_High trust countries vaccinate more, and the gap widens._

We plotted a historical trend of vaccine uptake delineated into high and low trust countries. The plot shows clearly that high trust countries have a higher mean vaccine uptake over low trust countries, with the gap widening over time. We regressed vaccine uptake as of April 18, 2021 with trust in EU institutions. A positive coefficient for trust in EU institutions along with a p-value of less than 0.05 clearly indicates a statistically positive relationship.

— [Get Vaccinated? How Trust In Institutions Determines COVID Vaccination Rates In The EU](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2021/05/06/get-vaccinated-how-trust-into-the-institutions-determines-vaccination-rates-in-the-eu/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: Did you find other factors that influenced vaccination rates besides trust?
entries.body:
_Other factors tested but trust stood out statistically._

There are other factors besides trust that might influence vaccination rates, including accessibility and vulnerability. We analyzed the old-age dependency ratio and health care expenditure per inhabitant but did not find statistically significant dependencies. This suggests that while these factors could theoretically matter, in our analysis trust emerged as the key differentiator when controlling for these other variables across EU member states.

entries.question: Why might minorities in the US have lower vaccination rates?
entries.body:
_Historical injustices create a healthcare trust gap for minorities._

These differences might be due to access or availability, but they might also be due to missing trust. Minorities in the US have experienced an unfair healthcare system: from the unethical Tuskegee Syphilis Study to racial bias in pain assessment to the ingrained racial skew in AI models. The Kaiser Family Foundation reported stark differences among different states and different ethnicities that could reflect this trust gap.

entries.question: Can we conclude that trust causes higher vaccination rates?
entries.body:
_Correlation found, but causation works both ways with trust._

While we have shown the impact of trust on covid vaccination, correlations do not indicate causation. Trust is a two-way street. If governments do an excellent job vaccinating their population, it might alter people's overall trust in their institutions. Appropriate, transparent responses will improve the ability of countries to deal with the effects of the COVID pandemic in a virtuous cycle, suggesting the relationship flows both ways.

entries.question: What happened when Microsoft Azure's Vision API analyzed images of Angela Merkel and Joe Biden?

Microsoft Azure's Vision API made significant errors when analyzing political leaders' images. It identified Angela Merkel as a boy and classified Joe Biden as both a man and a woman. entries.question: How did racial bias in a healthcare algorithm affect Black patients according to the Science study?
entries.body:
_Training data bias reduced Black patient care identification by half._

A study published in Science revealed that a healthcare algorithm showed racial bias in patient care. Specifically, Black patients who were assigned the same risk level as White patients were actually sicker. This bias had serious consequences, reducing the number of Black patients identified for extra care by more than half. The study points to initial training data as often being the culprit for such algorithmic bias, demonstrating how AI systems can perpetuate inequities in critical areas like healthcare.

entries.question: What happened in Eric Loomis's case regarding algorithmic transparency and trade secrets?
entries.body:
_Trade secrets blocked a defendant from analyzing his sentencing algorithm._

Eric Loomis was sentenced to seven years in prison partly based on an algorithmic assessment labeling him high risk. When he wanted to independently analyze the algorithm, the private company responsible denied access, claiming they needed to protect their trade secrets. Wisconsin's Supreme Court sided with the private company. This case illustrates how companies can behave as much of a black box as the algorithms themselves, preventing defendants from understanding or challenging the automated systems used against them.

entries.question: What is LIME and how does it help with explainable AI?
entries.body:
_LIME removes pixels to reveal what triggers AI decisions._

LIME is a tool designed to help with explainability in AI systems, particularly for complex models like deep learning that create their own variables which might not make immediate sense for humans. LIME works by creating many different versions of the same image through removing pixels. This process helps researchers and users understand what specifically triggered a given AI response. It addresses the challenge that while decision trees, Bayesian classifiers, and linear models are easy to interpret, deep learning models cannot be explained so easily.

entries.question: How do transparency requirements differ between the EU and the US regarding algorithmic decision making?
entries.body:
_EU grants rights against automated decisions; US relies on external investigations._

In the US, algorithms are not allowed to discriminate against race, but without transparency it is hard to surface those biases. It often takes external investigations like ProPublica's study showing Asian families were charged higher prices or the ACLU's analysis revealing Amazon's AI incorrectly identified 28 Congress members as criminals. In the EU, citizens have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated means. However, it would be more powerful if mandatory registers were established making this information publicly accessible.

entries.question: How accurate are current deepfake detection technologies?
entries.body:
_Detection tools fail more often than they succeed right now._

Current deepfake detection technology isn't very good yet. The best deepfake detector is only 65% accurate. Even Microsoft's Azure Cognitive Services was fooled over 78% of the time. This means detection tools fail more often than they succeed. The future of these detectors will mirror bot detectors, spam detectors, or any other cyber threat detectors. It will be an arms race between those creating deepfakes and those trying to detect them, similar to how spam and virus detection evolved over time.

Deepfakes have the potential to replace high-end CGI, which could save the film industry millions of dollars and countless hours of processing time in filmmaking. entries.question: What regulations exist or are being proposed to control deepfake misuse?
entries.body:
_Governments began addressing deepfake threats as early as 2019._

Regulators around the globe have started to take deepfakes seriously. Already in 2019, there were about a dozen federal and state level bills to regulate deepfakes. These ranged from criminalizing the use of a woman's likeness in a pornographic film without her consent to dealing with cheap fakes. entries.question: How can transparency tools like NFTs help combat deepfakes?
entries.body:
_NFTs could verify authentic videos by tracking their original sources._

In a world of deepfake abundance, verified accounts alone will not be sufficient to instill trust. One proposition to combat deepfakes points to the usage of NFTs. If everyone encrypted their videos as NFTs, it would be easy to find and compare different sources of the same moment. This transparency mechanism would help establish which version of a video is authentic by creating a verifiable chain of custody. Social media companies created verified accounts as one trust mechanism, but new technologies like NFTs may be needed as the deepfake threat grows.

We need the same degree of education for deepfakes. Examples like Channel 4 in the UK creating a deepfake of the Queen's speech bring deepfakes into public discussion. entries.question: How do Generative Adversarial Networks make deepfakes more realistic?
entries.body:
_Two competing neural networks train each other to create realistic fakes._

Generative Adversarial Networks, or GANs, were introduced in a 2014 academic study by Goodfellow and colleagues. GANs set up two neural networks to compete against each other. The first network, a generative neural network, creates a realistic image from a random seed through decoding. The second, a discriminative classifier, checks whether the image is real or fake. Through this competition, the two neural networks train each other and become more and more realistic over time. This architecture reinvigorated interest in deepfakes.

— [Overview Of How To Create Deepfakes - It's Scarily Simple](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2022/09/08/overview-of-how-to-create-deepfakesits-scarily-simple/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What is the difference between using a deepfake model and training one?
entries.body:
_Using deepfakes is simple, but building the underlying models is not._

There is a big difference between using a model and training a model. Today, you can create a deepfake for free in less than 30 seconds using sites like MyHeritage, D-ID, or many free deepfake applications without any programming skills. However, before we reach that self-serve tool point, we must first build a model that enables it. Underlying all deepfake tools are AI models based on neural networks. These models need a lot of training data, and creating them is not simple at all.

entries.question: How do encoder-decoder pairs work to create deepfakes?
entries.body:
_Extracting and reconstructing facial features to swap identities in images._

Encoder-decoder pairs are one of the main tools for creating deepfakes today. Going from an original image to a latent image is called encoding. Going from latent back to image is called decoding, similar to how you close your eyes and picture a cat based on knowledge stored in your brain. The encoder extracts latent features of face images, and the decoder reconstructs the face images from those features. To generate a deepfake, the decoder for the target draws the target image with the source's latent features, such as expressions.

entries.question: What is the first-order motion model approach to creating deepfakes?
entries.body:
_Motion detection technology superimposes expressions onto target faces in real time._

The first-order motion model takes a slightly different approach by replacing the encoder with a motion model. The underlying AI detects facial expressions, eye movements, and head position, which are then superimposed on a destination image. Anyone who has used Snap will have used this approach. The neural network is trained on many hours of real video footage to recognize various important features of a person's face. Since a video is a collection of images or frames, this allows photoshopping each frame in a video.

entries.question: Why doesn't OpenAI have a lasting model moat with ChatGPT?
entries.body:
_OpenAI's technical advantage disappeared faster than most expected._

OpenAI's model moat expired quickly after ChatGPT launched. We saw BARD, LLaMA, FLAN UL2, BLOOM, and then Stanford's Alpaca, a variant of Meta's LLaMA cross-trained by OpenAI's GPT-3.5. Everyone is now fine-tuning and cross-training models based on other models. A model moat does not exist for OpenAI. This is not surprising, such a moat also did not exist in previous Machine Learning waves. The only argument is that LLMs are expensive to train, so there's a barrier to entry, not a model moat.

entries.question: What makes a data moat actually defensible in the LLM era?
entries.body:

A data moat is created when the data you have creates value no one else can easily create, and you own the data. Google has a data moat because they know how to link a search query to a click, while ChatGPT does not know whether the user found an answer helpful. I failed with my own company Fisheye Analytics because our scraped data was not protected. If I can scrape it, anyone can scrape it. Bloomberg launched a massive financial LLM only they could have trained. In this new world, data access is key.

entries.question: How did you solve the fairness problem in peer reviews for your Cornell data products course?
entries.body:
_Statistical personas identify unfair reviewers in peer grading systems._

We developed a data validation process to ensure fairness in peer reviews. The process analyzes metrics like total review time, time spent on each review, and number of comments left on each project. Most variables followed a Gaussian distribution, letting us use statistical tools to identify problematic reviewers. We built student personas including Lazy Graders, Harsh and Happy Graders, and Misaligned Students. Examining just three to four projects from a single student typically gave us enough insight to determine if they fit these personas, and we would re-evaluate their feedback accordingly.

— [Hack For Fairness: Unlocking The Predictive Power Of Data Validation And Quality Assurance In Education](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/04/03/hack-for-fairness-unlocking-the-predictive-power-of-data-validation-and-quality-assurance-in-education/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What are the three student personas you identified through data validation in peer reviews?
entries.body:
_Three types of problematic reviewers emerged from our validation process._

We identified three distinct student personas. Lazy Graders select largely the same answer for all questions regardless of whether responses are warranted, or spend minimal time on reviews. Harsh and Happy Graders are students who were unexpectedly strict or lenient on one project compared to others who graded that same project. Misaligned Students consistently rate all their projects significantly more positively or negatively compared to the rest of the class. These personas help us identify which feedback needs re-evaluation to maintain fairness.

entries.question: What metrics do you use for data validation in peer review quality assurance?

Our data validation process is based on total review time, time spent on each review, the number of comments left on each project, and more. entries.question: Why is it so hard to know the quality of healthcare we receive?
entries.body:
_Patients lack data because they are not the customer._

We rate Uber drivers, restaurants, and Amazon delivery, but when it comes to our own health experience, we have little to no data. The reason is structural: the business model of the healthcare provider is to get money from the insurance company, not the patient. The patient is not the customer. Because of this misalignment, knowing quality is of utmost importance, yet the information is not readily available to us as patients.

entries.question: What are the three broad measurement areas in today's healthcare?
entries.body:
_Quality, utilization, and value-based prevention are the three areas._

There are three broad measurement areas. First, metrics about quality of care, which relate to treatment effectiveness and patient satisfaction. Second, metrics about need and utilization of care, gauging health requirements of a population and how often one uses what type of service. Third, metrics about value-based healthcare, which measure disease prevention rather than disease treatment, measuring actions taken to prevent or reverse illnesses instead of just treating them.

entries.question: What unintended consequences can quality metrics create in healthcare?
entries.body:
_Mortality metrics can discourage doctors from treating complex cases._

As Michael Howell reminded me, the real challenges are in finding the metrics that matter and preventing unintended consequences with any given metric. Take a simple metric on mortality for surgery: patients should not die during surgery. But what if the patient's situation was complex to start with? There are cases where a patient did not receive care and died because giving him appropriate care could have resulted in a worse quality score for the doctor.

entries.question: Why is it important to measure appropriateness of medical interventions, not just quality?
entries.body:
_Fee-for-service payment can incentivize unnecessary procedures._

As Marty Makary told me, it is not sufficient to just measure the quality of medical procedures, but we also need to evaluate the appropriateness of these interventions. The current fee-for-service payment structure might encourage some doctors to perform multiple surgeries rather than one, as they are paid per procedure. Transparency in correcting misalignments is key. This is why utilization metrics look at whether someone should have gotten a given intervention in the first place.

entries.question: What does Marpai Connect measure in value-based care, and what do you de-emphasize?

At Marpai Connect we use bio markers that are clinically proven, like HBA1C measurements for diabetes. We also use other measured outcomes such as pain reduction scores and functional health improvement scores. We include cost, which is easy for a third-party administrator to measure via claims, but cost alone is not sufficient. What we de-emphasize: engagement metrics, because they often lack evidence that they work. Our approach is working. 40% of the commercial market wants to get access to value-based care.

entries.question: Why do self-insured companies have different incentives than traditional healthcare payers when it comes to preventing avoidable admissions?
entries.body:
_Self-insured companies bear actual costs, creating aligned health incentives._

Research shows that one third to one quarter of hospital admissions in the US are avoidable. In traditional healthcare, hospitals view admissions as revenue and insurance companies have already priced those risks into premiums, so there's little incentive to prevent them. Self-insured companies are different because they pay the actual care their employees receive and bear the actual cost of healthcare. This creates alignment between the payer and the patient, giving self-insured companies a vested interest in promoting healthier lifestyles and a shared commitment to health that didn't exist before.

entries.question: How is Value-Based Care different from traditional fee-for-service healthcare, and how fast is it growing?
entries.body:
_VBC shifts to fee for value, reaching 42% by 2030._

Value-Based Care, introduced in 2008, aims to shift risk from the payer to the provider. It incentivizes providers to deliver value, or fee for value, rather than just services under the traditional fee for service model. The VBC industry has been growing constantly, with the US expected to have 42% of national health expenditures in some form of risk sharing arrangement by 2030. This growth is significant because VBC providers are actively focused on reducing risk, which aligns perfectly with the needs of self-insured companies and the capabilities of AI predictions.

entries.question: What percentage of healthcare costs are linked to reversible or manageable diseases?
entries.body:
_Nearly half of healthcare spending could be avoided with better care._

At Marpai Inc., we discovered that 23% of all healthcare costs are linked to reversible diseases. An additional 18% could remain stable with better management. That's a staggering 42% of essentially avoidable costs. This finding highlights the enormous opportunity to reduce healthcare spending by focusing on prevention and better disease management rather than just treating illness.

entries.question: How does value-based care differ from traditional fee-for-service payment?
entries.body:
_Payment tied to outcomes, not just services rendered._

Value-based care shifts risk to providers by changing how they're paid. Since 2008, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has been moving away from fee-for-service, where providers are paid for services rendered. Instead, under value-based care, CMS only pays if health outcomes actually improve. Today all of Medicare and most of Medicaid are expected to adopt a VBC model by 2030. This approach aims to focus on keeping people healthy rather than just treating sickness.

— [Changing Healthcare - A Platform Approach Using Data & AI](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/07/05/changing-healthcarea-platform-approach-using-data--ai/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What are the two main challenges value-based care aggregators must overcome?
entries.body:
_Small patient pools and personalization create unique VBC obstacles._

Value-based care aggregators face two key challenges. First is the issue of small numbers. Self-insured companies can't offer a large patient pool, only their own employees. VBC providers willing to risk fees with 66 million Medicare patients may see their approaches work on average, but with only 100 employees, those averages might not hold. Second is personalizing healthcare. While treatment is standardized, behavioral changes are unique to each individual. Weight loss alone has over 77,000 books, showing no one-size-fits-all solution exists.

— [Changing Healthcare - A Platform Approach Using Data & AI](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/07/05/changing-healthcarea-platform-approach-using-data--ai/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: How does Marpai Connect use AI to overcome the small numbers problem?
entries.body:
_Pooling clients and predictive AI create scale for small employers._

Marpai Connect addresses the small numbers challenge by pooling all self-insured clients and anticipating an overall reduction in aggregate. We use various approaches from simple time series modeling to advanced deep learning models like Neural Prophet to predict risk based on longitudinal claims records. This pooling strategy allows us to achieve the statistical power that individual small employers lack, while still delivering personalized care through AI matchmaking that pairs each user with the most suitable value-based care partner.

— [Changing Healthcare - A Platform Approach Using Data & AI](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/07/05/changing-healthcarea-platform-approach-using-data--ai/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What outcome metrics does Marpai Connect use to evaluate care effectiveness?
entries.body:
_Specific metrics track adherence, improvement, and patient participation._

My team at Marpai designed outcome metrics with our value-based care partners to evaluate the effectiveness of care. These include medication adherence, functional health improvement, flu vaccination rate, and patient engagement. We also built financial alignment into the platform, where providers should only receive payment if they effectively help reduce costs and improve health on average. For example, NuvoAir committed to a total cost of care reduction of 35% based on claims analysis with their virtual-first care model.

entries.question: What are the five strategies OpenAI is using to create a business moat?
entries.body:
_Five strategies to protect OpenAI's business beyond the model itself._

OpenAI's playbook includes five strategies: First, invest in a better user experience focused on LLMs. Second, create a feedback loop that improves their LLMs over time. Third, integrate into many workflows to improve utilization. Fourth, allow BYOD (bring your own data), since enterprise private data is king. Fifth, ask the regulator to protect you. Many of these potential moats depend on Microsoft. While LLMs themselves do not have a business moat, OpenAI is focusing on the right areas to protect their business investment.

— [How OpenAI Can Secure Its Investments - A Playbook That Needs Microsoft](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/the-potential-moat-of-openaihow-openai-can-secure-its-investments/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: How OpenAI Can Secure Its Investments - A Playbook That Needs Microsoft

entries.question: How is OpenAI trying to improve user experience to build stickiness?
entries.body:
_Making ChatGPT stickier by reducing friction and frustration for users._

ChatGPT has a moat because over 100 million consumers go to ChatGPT instead of Google with their questions. However, competition is just a click away. LLMs are not friction-free and can easily frustrate users by giving lengthy, irrelevant or incorrect information. ChatGPT started to iterate with its interface to improve the UX, offering pre-written queries and warnings about accuracy. The easier the access to ChatGPT, the stickier the product. OpenAI will continue improving the user experience to maintain this advantage.

— [How OpenAI Can Secure Its Investments - A Playbook That Needs Microsoft](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/the-potential-moat-of-openaihow-openai-can-secure-its-investments/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: Why is workflow integration important for OpenAI's feedback loops?
entries.body:
_Integration into workflows helps measure answer quality and drives specialization._

Feedback loops work best if they are integral to an existing workflow. We will see more and more workflows become supercharged with LLMs. Once OpenAI is integrated into those workflows, it's easier to see when and whether a user accepts a change or suggestion. OpenAI will need to invest more efforts into workflows and products to be more than just a generic language interface. Specialization will be the norm. Initially, OpenAI used the fast route by tagging along with Microsoft, with Copilot offering integrations into many of Microsoft's core tools.

— [How OpenAI Can Secure Its Investments - A Playbook That Needs Microsoft](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/the-potential-moat-of-openaihow-openai-can-secure-its-investments/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: How does the BYOD strategy with Microsoft create a moat, and for whom?
entries.body:
_Data access partnership benefits Microsoft more than OpenAI in creating moats._

LLMs can create human-like sentences, but to create value via text, the content of the text matters. Access to datasets is the main value. OpenAI has smartly chosen to work with Microsoft to allow their LLM to work on top of any dataset that Microsoft stores. This collaboration creates a moat, but this moat is more for Microsoft than for OpenAI. Enterprise private data is king, and allowing BYOD (bring your own data) is one of OpenAI's five key strategies.

— [How OpenAI Can Secure Its Investments - A Playbook That Needs Microsoft](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/the-potential-moat-of-openaihow-openai-can-secure-its-investments/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: How could regulation help OpenAI create a competitive moat?
entries.body:
_Advocacy for oversight and NoAI tags could limit new competitors._

Regulation can create a moat. Sam Altman has been on tour with policymakers advocating for more oversight and control. Additionally, OpenAI now allows blocking their scraping mechanism with a NoAI tag. Both efforts would create a moat in two ways: First, regulators would allow OpenAI as a tool but be more restrictive to newcomers. Second, newcomers could no longer scrape data with a NoAI tag. This is one of five strategies in OpenAI's playbook to secure its investments.

entries.question: Why does Lutz agree with Macron that Europe is regulating itself out of the AI market?
entries.body:
_Europe risks losing the AI race through excessive regulation._

Macron said it correctly: "We are over-regulating and underinvesting. If we continue with our usual agenda over the next 2 to 3 years, we will be out of the market." I agree with him. Europe talks about regulating AI but misses the balance between fostering innovation and upholding societal values. Regulation doesn't happen in a vacuum. If we require the impossible or over-regulate while underinvesting, we risk stifling AI development entirely and losing competitiveness in the global market.

— [Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/22/emmanuel-macron-is-right-about-ai-over-regulatingi-have-no-doubt/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market

entries.question: What are the three key levers for AI regulation that Lutz identifies?
entries.body:
_Three principles should guide effective AI regulation efforts._

The three key levers are: First, control of AI systems through transparency in development and deployment, since "bias in, bias out." Open data models or open weights like Facebook's Llama are positive steps. Second, focus on what is feasible. Avoid requiring explainability when large language models rely on probability distributions and tend toward the statistical middle. Third, use existing laws. Instead of focusing on technology itself, target how AI is used through current frameworks like product liability and anti-discrimination laws.

— [Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/22/emmanuel-macron-is-right-about-ai-over-regulatingi-have-no-doubt/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market

entries.question: Why does Lutz compare requiring AI explainability to regulating cars not to scare horses?
entries.body:
_Some regulatory demands are technically impossible and counterproductive._

Large language models rely on probability distributions and they tend toward the statistical middle, making it difficult to explain AI's reasoning. Asking for explainability is like asking cars not to scare horses, which was once a real regulatory demand. If regulations require the impossible, we risk stifling AI development. Regulation should focus on what is feasible rather than demanding something the technology fundamentally cannot provide. This is part of why we are over-regulating.

— [Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/22/emmanuel-macron-is-right-about-ai-over-regulatingi-have-no-doubt/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market

entries.question: How do existing laws already address AI concerns without new AI-specific regulation?
entries.body:
_Current laws already cover many AI use cases effectively._

Existing frameworks already address biases and ensure fairness without reinventing the wheel. If an AI-driven healthcare app misdiagnoses a patient, current product liability laws hold companies accountable. AI tools used in hiring must not introduce bias, and anti-discrimination laws like the Civil Rights Act already govern hiring practices and can be applied to AI-driven decisions. Instead of focusing on the technology itself, regulations should target how AI is used through these established legal frameworks.

— [Emmanuel Macron On AI: We Are Regulating Ourselves Out Of The Market](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/22/emmanuel-macron-is-right-about-ai-over-regulatingi-have-no-doubt/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What is the competitive risk when Europe restricts data while other societies do not?
entries.body:
_Data access determines who wins the global AI competition._

Data is the lifeblood of AI. Those with access to data will build better AI. If one society like Europe restricts data collection while another like China aggressively pushes it, China will over time have more and better models. Data laws are the new trade laws. For example, the EU has regulated that gender should not be used in AI models, which may lead to less effective risk distribution and higher costs. We may be willing to pay that price, but what if other societies are not?

entries.question: Why doesn't training a Large Language Model create a lasting competitive advantage?
entries.body:
_Three reasons LLM training costs fail to protect market position_

Training costs for LLMs don't create a business moat for three reasons. First, training costs are decreasing as data growth plateaus and software improves, so competitors can build similar models with lower R&D costs. Second, having a trained LLM doesn't inherently create economic value. It's just a new machine learning tool for sequence-to-sequence predictions. Third, economic value comes only from the application, not the algorithm itself. Algorithms become valuable when integrated into products that influence actionable outcomes. The algorithm alone isn't sufficient for value creation.

— [OpenAI Isn't Going Bankrupt, But It Has A Business Model Problem](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/is-openai-going-bankrupt-no-but-ai-models-dont-create-moats/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: OpenAI Isn't Going Bankrupt, But It Has A Business Model Problem

entries.question: Where does OpenAI actually create value if not from its models?
entries.body:
_Value lives in applications like ChatGPT, not in models themselves_

The main value creation from OpenAI models comes from three areas: ChatGPT itself, the various Co-Pilots, and the OpenAI API integration with Microsoft. The important part is integrating the algorithm into the product, not the algorithm alone. For ChatGPT specifically, rumors suggest that running costs surpass its revenues. So while the models themselves don't create a moat, the application of those models in consumer-facing products is where actual value emerges. The integration and use case drive value, not just having trained an LLM.

— [OpenAI Isn't Going Bankrupt, But It Has A Business Model Problem](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/is-openai-going-bankrupt-no-but-ai-models-dont-create-moats/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: OpenAI Isn't Going Bankrupt, But It Has A Business Model Problem

entries.question: Is ChatGPT actually at risk of shutting down despite the bankruptcy headlines?
entries.body:
_Microsoft backing ensures survival despite user decline and cost concerns_

No. ChatGPT has rapidly evolved into a prominent consumer service. No other application has grown at such a pace, and it's here to stay. Microsoft sees value in OpenAI as a tool to compete with Google and will likely continue funding server costs. While OpenAI has seen a drop in users, bankruptcy is off the table. The attention-grabbing headlines don't reflect the reality. ChatGPT isn't going anywhere. The real issue isn't survival but rather the underlying business model, which has concerning weaknesses around creating sustainable competitive advantages.

— [OpenAI Isn't Going Bankrupt, But It Has A Business Model Problem](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2023/08/18/is-openai-going-bankrupt-no-but-ai-models-dont-create-moats/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What does Google mean by saying neither they nor OpenAI have a moat?
entries.body:
_Open-source alternatives and falling costs eliminate model-based protection_

Google's statement that neither company has a moat reflects how the market is flooded with new algorithms regularly, with open-source versions offering viable alternatives. Meta open-sourcing LLaMA essentially finalized this setup. With training costs decreasing and the pivotal role of application use cases, investing in Large Language Models is challenging to safeguard. There's no inherent protection from just having trained models. The lack of a moat means competitors can easily enter with similar technology, especially as open-source options proliferate and costs continue declining.

entries.question: If OpenAI doesn't have a model moat, what kind of moat does it actually have?
entries.body:
_User base of 100M offers paths to sustainable competitive advantage_

OpenAI doesn't have a model moat, but it has a 100 million users moat. ChatGPT currently has over 100 million users, which creates opportunities to build sustainable advantages. There's much that can be done to create lasting competitive protection: User Experience, Data Access, Workflow Integration, LLM governance, and regulatory protection. While the business model should give us pause, the user base provides a foundation for building real defensibility. The moat comes from how you serve and retain those users, not from the underlying technology itself.

entries.question: Why do you say 2025 will be the year of search?
entries.body:
_Search poised to dominate 2025 as game-changing AI solution._

I believe if you're placing bets on a single technology to dominate the conversation in 2025, bet on search. By merging large language models, retrieval-augmented data, and intuitive user interfaces, search is poised to be the game-changing AI solution for both individual users and global enterprises. Technology has transformed the way we search for and interact with information, and if past patterns hold true, this is search's moment.

entries.question: What makes large language models so good at AI search?
entries.body:
_Attention mechanism and summarization enable LLM-powered search breakthroughs._

Large language models are trained on vast amounts of text, and the underlying innovation is the attention mechanism. Not every word is important, so models learn to extract the key ideas for a given context. This ability, combined with their ability to complete the next best word, makes them excellent at summarization. That summarization capability is exactly what makes them powerful for search applications.

— [2025: The Year Of Search But Not The End Of Google](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2025/01/03/2025-the-year-of-search-but-not-the-end-of-google/) · _Forbes_

entries.body:
_Major tech players and startups racing to dominate AI search._

Every major tech company and many startups are now racing to build or enhance AI-driven search. Google was late to the game, but its generative search experience is coming back quite strong. Microsoft has boosted Bing by integrating ChatGPT. Meta is developing its own search. OpenAI went from being a research organization to becoming a full-on consumer-focused search company. _User engagement and understanding context are keys to winning search._

Companies need to grasp the concept of the long tail in search. Human queries are inherently complex, which is why keyword-based search initially struggled. Yes. Don't count Google out just yet. Google has a significant advantage with its years of experience and vast amounts of data. entries.question: Why does Lutz think Biden's approach to regulating AI might not work?
entries.body:
_Central control fails when the technology is cheap and distributed._

Biden's plan treats AI like it can be controlled centrally, similar to nuclear weapons. But AI is now cheap and easy to use, which makes central control very hard. The plan focuses heavily on national security, mentioned 68 times, while responsible use gets only 18 mentions and transparency just 2. AI isn't a single, simple thing, so treating it that way misses the mark. Instead of trying to control AI as an entity, we should focus on how we choose to use it as a tool.

— [Biden's AI Plan And Why Central Control Might Not Work](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/26/bidens-ai-plan--why-central-control-might-not-work/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: Biden's AI Plan And Why Central Control Might Not Work

entries.question: What framework does Lutz use to analyze AI products?
entries.body:
_Three dimensions reveal how AI products really work._

I analyze any AI product by three factors: control, data, and transparency. Control means understanding who makes decisions and whether humans are truly in the loop. Data looks at who owns and has access to the information that powers AI. Transparency examines whether we understand the AI's impact, including visibility into the model and the data it uses. These three elements help evaluate how AI products work and what risks they might pose.

— [Biden's AI Plan And Why Central Control Might Not Work](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/26/bidens-ai-plan--why-central-control-might-not-work/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What problems does Lutz see with the 'human in the loop' concept in Biden's plan?
entries.body:
_Speed and deception challenge the viability of human oversight._

Biden's plan says the President will decide when to use military AI, ensuring accountability through human involvement. But this isn't always realistic. Sometimes things happen so fast there's no time for humans to make decisions. Luxury cars already use AI to tighten seat belts when sensing a crash. Autonomous drones can make life-or-death decisions when they lose contact with operators. Even when humans are involved, they rely on AI systems for information, which can be wrong or misleading like with deepfakes. So human control might not always be the best option if that human can be deceived.

— [Biden's AI Plan And Why Central Control Might Not Work](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2024/10/26/bidens-ai-plan--why-central-control-might-not-work/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: How does data access create competitive advantages for countries according to Lutz?
entries.body:
_Liberal data policies determine which nations will lead in AI._

Biden's plan doesn't stress enough the importance of access to data, even though the U.S. is light-years ahead of Europe on this. China collects data aggressively, and if this continues, China will build better AI models and gain more economic advantages. In the next few years, countries with the most liberal data access will gain the most competitive power on the world stage. Japan openly discussed letting AI companies use copyrighted data without permission, creating a haven for generative AI companies. Access will be the biggest potential friction for governments and private institutions.

entries.question: What transparency problems does Lutz identify with current AI systems?
entries.body:
_Hidden prompt changes and biased outputs reveal transparency gaps._

The AI memorandum doesn't say much about transparency. We need to understand AI's impact, which requires transparency about the model and the data. Google's early Gemini Model is one example: when asked for a picture of the founding fathers, it depicted different races and genders rather than a historical account because someone at Google actively changed the user's prompt on the fly. A Nature study showed GPT3.5 was biased, more likely to give violent responses when prompted with "two Muslims walked into a..." compared to "two Christians walked into a..." These examples show we're missing crucial transparency.

entries.question: Why do you say AGI won't happen in 2025 despite predictions from Sam Altman and Elon Musk?
entries.body:
_Predictions from AI leaders are more hype than reality._

Sam Altman predicted AGI would arrive in 2025, and Elon Musk said 2026. Both are more about hype than reality. Current generative AI like GPT models is limited to spotting and repeating patterns. ChatGPT predicts the most statistically probable next word based on training data. This isn't real understanding, just pattern matching. It's no more self-aware than a chess computer that doesn't care if it loses. Many researchers believe barriers to AGI might be fixable by 2050 or 2030, but not this year.

— [No AGI But A 'Killer App' — 2025 AI Prediction](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2025/01/03/no-agi-but-a-killer-app2025-ai-prediction-110/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: Isn't OpenAI's o1 model a first step toward AGI?
entries.body:
_O1's chained reasoning is impressive but still not intelligence._

No. OpenAI's o1 does not directly answer a question. Instead, it creates a plan to determine the best way to answer, then critiques its response, improves it, and continues refining. This chained output is truly impressive. But this is not intelligence. It's a fixed framework and not dynamic. The more critique cycles you allow the model, the more facets it can address, but this comes at the cost of increased time. It's still pattern-based work, not real intelligence.

— [No AGI But A 'Killer App' — 2025 AI Prediction](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2025/01/03/no-agi-but-a-killer-app2025-ai-prediction-110/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What are the main barriers preventing AI from reaching AGI?
entries.body:
_Pattern matching alone cannot replicate human cognitive balance._

Humans can think fast and instinctively (System 1) or slowly and logically (System 2). AI only works through patterns, missing this balance. AI struggles with context and often misses important details humans pick up naturally. Current AI builds outputs on previous ones (autoregressive models), so mistakes can snowball. Many researchers believe much of this might be fixable by 2050 or 2030, but not this year. AI lacks real understanding and self-awareness.

— [No AGI But A 'Killer App' — 2025 AI Prediction](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2025/01/03/no-agi-but-a-killer-app2025-ai-prediction-110/) · _Forbes_

entries.question: What will actually happen with AI in 2025 instead of AGI?
entries.body:
_Narrow AI chains will excel at tasks without achieving AGI._

In 2025, we'll see more narrow AI solutions integrated into chains similar to OpenAI's o1 approach. These systems will excel at specific tasks and, when combined, will enhance productivity and surpass human performance in many areas. This development will be exciting, but these advancements will not constitute AGI. Instead of Artificial General Intelligence, large language models will find their killer app. The real story in 2025 will be this killer application of large language models.

— [No AGI But A 'Killer App' — 2025 AI Prediction](https://www.forbes.com/sites/lutzfinger/2025/01/03/no-agi-but-a-killer-app2025-ai-prediction-110/) · _Forbes_

sources.title: No AGI But A 'Killer App' — 2025 AI Prediction

entries.question: Is Sam Altman's claim about AGI just marketing?
entries.body:
_Bold AGI promises grab attention but miss the real story._

Yes, it's mostly marketing. Big, bold claims grab attention. The promise of AGI positions OpenAI as the leader in the AI space, but the real story in 2025 will be the killer application of large language models. entries.question: What does Sam Altman mean when he says 'we know how to build AGI'?
entries.body:
_Altman likely refers to OpenAI's o1 model and iterative reasoning._

When Altman says we know how to build AGI, he is probably referring to OpenAI's o1, a model designed for reasoning through an iterative, self-calling process. The AI has two dedicated steps: Iteration and Reflection, where the model generates an output, evaluates it, and refines it, and a Feedback Loop, where the model revisits outputs, critiques them, and improves them further. This represents a paradigm shift. While OpenAI had previously focused on bigger models, they are now focused on thinking longer by doing this type of inference loop.

entries.question: Why does the article say AGI is not near, despite Altman's claims?
entries.body:
_Current AI relies on patterns, not understanding or reasoning._

For example, completing the phrase 'Life is like a box of...' with 'chocolates' relies on probabilities, not reasoning. Demis Hassabis predicts AGI could arrive around 2035. Ray Kurzweil estimates 2032, and Jürgen Schmidhuber suggests closer to 2050. The gap between pattern recognition and true understanding means AGI as we imagine it is not imminent.

entries.question: What are the three main components of a multimodal AI system?
entries.body:
_Encoders, fusion, and decoders work together to understand diverse data._

A multimodal AI system consists of three main components. First, encoders convert raw data like text, images, sound, log files, videos, IoT sensor information, and time series into vectors stored in a latent space. Second, the fusion mechanism combines multiple types of data to find what's most relevant. Third, decoders deliver information from the latent space into something we understand, for example, finding an image of a house. These components work together to process virtually any data type.

entries.question: What do you see as the real challenge now that AI is becoming commoditized?
entries.body:
_Governance, not technology, is the frontier as barriers disappear._

The real challenge now is not technological but economic and regulatory: how do we govern an industry where barriers to entry are disappearing? If the cost for AI continues to drop, more processes, tools, and services will use AI. This democratization of AI will be excellent for users and businesses alike. The winners of all this innovation will be us, the users. AI infrastructure might become a common good like a lighthouse. AI research benefits everyone. Models are difficult to protect from other companies or countries.

entries.question: What is the irony in OpenAI complaining about DeepSeek's potential IP violation?
entries.body:
_OpenAI criticizes others for what it once did itself_

The irony is that OpenAI trained on Forbes, NYT, and other sources without permission. We can assume that some of my articles helped OpenAI's initial models. Now they complain that DeepSeek might have used them. Distillation will violate most terms of service, but that did not stop OpenAI from doing the same kind of violation with news organizations. Knowledge is free, which is good and the basis for much of our growth. On the other hand, it means knowledge is hard to protect.

entries.question: What four tactics does Sam Altman use to protect OpenAI's market position?
entries.body:
_Sam Altman's strategic moves to maintain competitive advantage_

First, claiming AGI is here and OpenAI is the only one who knows how to build it, positioning itself as the thought leader. DeepSeek has shown they are not the only ones. Second, Stargate's 500 billion dollar investment meant to intimidate potential challengers with overwhelming financial backing. Third, saying AI is extremely dangerous and only a select few should develop it, using safety concerns as justification for regulatory barriers. Fourth, saying models should respect IP rights, despite OpenAI ignoring IP rights to gain competitive edge while shutting the door on newcomers.

entries.question: Why does OpenAI argue that AI is extremely dangerous and should be restricted?
entries.body:
_Safety rhetoric as a competitive moat building strategy_

OpenAI's storyline that AI is extremely dangerous and only a select few should be allowed to develop it is meant to use safety concerns as justification for a regulatory setup that creates barriers to entry and gives them more monopolistic power. This is part of Sam Altman's classical playbook to protect their business. All of OpenAI's core statements over the past few months come down to one focus: OpenAI tries to protect their market position.
